articles.title_original: Two-Dimensional Memristors: Materials, Switching Physics, Architectures, and Computing Applications
articles.title_en: Review Highlights 2D Memristors for Neuromorphic Computing
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract For the upcoming generation of non-volatile memory, neuromorphic computing, and in-memory artificial intelligence (AI) hardware, two-dimensional (2D) material-based memristors have emerged as a promising device type. Their van der Waals (vdW) interfaces, atomic-scale thickness, and tunable electronic characteristics enable remarkable control over resistive switching mechanisms. They have an advantage over conventional bulk oxide memristors in terms of device uniformity, scalability, and power efficiency. An overview of recent developments in 2D memristive technologies is provided in this review, which also discusses material systems like black phosphorus, hexagonal boron nitride, graphene derivatives, transition metal dichalcogenides, and new 2D ferroelectrics. Additionally, it covers important resistive switching mechanisms such as interface-modulated switching, electrochemical metallization, defect and vacancy migration, and phase-transition-driven behavior. The effectiveness of various device architectures, such as planar and vertical structures, vdW heterostructures, and large-scale crossbar arrays, for in-memory computing is examined. Furthermore, neuromorphic characteristics such as very low-energy matrix-vector multiplication, spiking neural networks, analog weight modulation, and synaptic plasticity are emphasized. Important problems pertaining to endurance, environmental stability, variability, and large-area growth are explored, along with fresh approaches to these problems. Finally, future directions that highlight the revolutionary potential of 2D memristors for AI, edge computing, and next-generation memory technologies are described, including 3D integration, atomically engineered defects, and ultra-flexible neuromorphic systems.
articles.summary_en: A review examines graphene derivatives and other two-dimensional materials for non-volatile memory, in-memory AI, and neuromorphic hardware. It assesses switching mechanisms, device architectures, scalability, energy efficiency, and remaining challenges including variability, endurance, stability, and large-area growth.

articles.title_original: Électronique flexible et portable en utilisant de matériaux 1D-2D
articles.title_en: Inkjet-Printed Graphene RF Devices Demonstrated on Paper
articles.excerpt_original: Over the past years, flexible and wearable electronics have attracted growing interest due to their ability to function reliably even when undergoing significant deformation, as well as their wide range potential applications. Inkjet printing is one of the most promising techniques for large-area fabrication of flexible and wearable electronics. The challenge with this technique lies in the precision and print quality, in particular when it comes to RF circuits. The main objective of this study is to develop high- resolution flexible RF devices and in particular to use water-based 2D materials to fabricate field-effect transistors, all using inkjet printing technology. Thus, this work focused on the design, fabrication and RF characterisation of printed RF devices, such as CPW transmission lines, bandpass filters and CPW hybrid couplers, as well as an exploratory study focusing in particular on the use of graphene and hBN for the fabrication of printed field-effect transistors. The mobility of the printed graphene was around 1.8 cm²V⁻¹s⁻¹. Using a non-commercial inkjet printer prototype and paper substrate, several RF devices with micro-scale precision were fabricated, achieving uniform spacing as small as 9 µm and conductor widths of 50 µm. A band-pass filter, using two-layers printing approach and centred at 25 GHz, fabricated from this technology achieves an insertion loss of −5 dB in the pass-band. In addition, a CPW hybrid coupler with bridges has been successfully printed. Paper was chosen as a sustainable and flexible substrate. The printed CPWs demonstrate attenuation of 0.5 dB/mm at 10 GHz and 1.1 dB/mm at 50 GHz.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed water-based inkjet-printed flexible RF components and explored graphene and hBN field-effect transistors on paper substrates. The technology achieved 9 µm spacing, 25 GHz band-pass filtering, and low measured transmission-line attenuation, supporting flexible high-frequency electronics applications.

articles.title_original: Spin-valley coupling and spin-polarized transport in a two-dimensional altermagnetic Cr2WS4 monolayer
articles.title_en: Cr₂WS₄ Monolayer Shows Strain-Tunable Spin Transport
articles.excerpt_original: Altermagnetism, characterized by momentum-dependent spin-splitting without net magnetization, attracts considerable attention due to its unique symmetry-governed electronic structures and potential applications in spintronic devices. Here, based on first-principles calculations, we identify Cr2WS4 monolayer as a two-dimensional tetragonal altermagnetic (AM) semiconductor. It exhibits a pair of energy degenerate valleys at X and Y points around the valence band maximum with opposite spin polarizations. We demonstrate that the degeneracy of X/Y valleys can be removed by in-plane uniaxial strain. Furthermore, the direction- and doping-dependent spin transport has been explored. Remarkably, we find that electron doping can lead to nearly 100% spin polarized currents in Cr2WS4 monolayer. These findings highlight the potential of AM semiconductors for low-power spintronic and spin-logic applications.
articles.summary_en: First-principles calculations identify Cr₂WS₄ as a two-dimensional altermagnetic semiconductor with spin-polarized valleys. Uniaxial strain controls valley degeneracy, while electron doping produces nearly fully spin-polarized currents, indicating potential for low-power spintronic and spin-logic devices.

articles.title_original: Antiferromagnetic semiconductor NdAsTe: A new member of LnAsTe (Ln = Lanthanoids) compounds
articles.title_en: NdAsTe Identified as an Antiferromagnetic Semiconductor with Low-Temperature Magnetoresistance Crossover
articles.excerpt_original: Rare-earth-based intermetallic compounds are at the forefront of materials science, providing valuable insights into the interplay among magnetism, topology, and structural correlations. The interesting properties of these materials, driven by localized 4f -electrons, strong spin-orbit coupling (SOC), and crystal electric field (CEF) effect, make them a focal point in solid-state physics for designing advanced functional materials. We have synthesized NdAsTe using the solid-state reaction route and explored the temperature and field-dependent magnetic properties, which demonstrate long-range antiferromagnetic (AFM) ordering below T N ≃ 2.4 K. The low-temperature Curie-Weiss temperature θ CW ≃ -1.89 K implies a net AFM interaction between the Nd 3+ ions. Furthermore, the isothermal magnetization data exhibit signatures of spin-reorientation of the AFM-aligned spins at T < T N , corroborated through magnetic entropy studies. The signature of AFM transition is also manifested as a peak at T N in the temperature-dependent specific heat which gradually shifts towards lower temperatures at higher applied fields. The derived parameters from specific heat data suggest the presence of strong electronic correlations in NdAsTe. The magnetic susceptibility and specific heat data suggest that the magnetic ground state is a Kramers' doublet with effective spin J eff = 1/2 at low temperatures. The electrical transport study revealed the semiconducting nature with a band gap of 70 meV. Furthermore, the low temperature (T < 20 K) magnetotransport studies unfold a crossover from positive to negative magnetoresistance behavior.
articles.summary_en: Researchers synthesized NdAsTe and found long-range antiferromagnetic ordering below approximately 2.4 K, with a 70 meV band gap and strong electronic correlations. Its low-temperature magnetotransport changes from positive to negative magnetoresistance, highlighting potential relevance for semiconductor and magnetic-materials research.

articles.title_original: Dopant-induced modifications of the optical properties of GaSe
articles.title_en: Fe doping tunes GaSe optical and magnetic properties
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Doping plays a crucial role in tailoring the electronic, optical, and magnetic properties of semiconductors, enabling control of carrier dynamics and the formation of functional states for optoelectronic applications. We investigate the influence of Fe dopants on the optical properties of GaSe crystals using photoluminescence (PL) spectroscopy under varying excitation power, temperature, and magnetic field. Fe incorporation introduces multiple sharp emission lines in addition to intrinsic excitonic transitions, including free and localised excitons. Power-and temperature-dependent measurements indicate that these emission features are associated with Fe-related dopant centres (Fe-bound excitons). Magneto-PL measurements reveal two distinct families of g-factors, enabling the identification of intrinsic excitonic transitions and Fe-induced defect states. These results demonstrate that Fe doping creates optically and magnetically active centres in GaSe, providing insight into defect-related excitonic processes and their potential relevance for magneto-optoelectronic and quantum photonic applications.
articles.summary_en: Researchers show that iron dopants introduce sharp emission lines and Fe-bound excitons in gallium selenide crystals. The findings clarify defect-related excitonic behavior relevant to magneto-optoelectronic and quantum photonic applications.

articles.title_original: Hands-on fabrication of 2D material field-effect transistors for the classroom using off-the-shelf ionic gel
articles.title_en: Classroom fabrication method enables MoS₂ field-effect transistors
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract We introduce a hands-on experimental method that enables students to fabricate and operate van der Waals semiconductor-based field-effect transistors (FETs) using readily available materials and minimal infrastructure. The approach is based on ionic-gel gating using commercially available hydrogel conductors originally developed for muscle electrostimulation devices. For device fabrication we rely on commercially available thin-film interdigitated electrode arrays and for the semiconductor channel, we deposited MoS2 flakes produced by high-throughput mechanical exfoliation. By avoiding the need for cleanroom processing, vacuum deposition, or custom electrolytes, this method allows functional FETs based on van der Waals materials to be realized in a standard teaching laboratory. The experiment is well suited for undergraduate and early graduate courses and is intended to complement concepts introduced in electronics and solid-state physics by providing students with first-hand experience in the fabrication and electrical characterization of emerging electronic devices. Representative electrical measurements demonstrate gate-dependent modulation of the channel conductance and illustrate characteristic features of ionic-gated transistor operation. Overall, the proposed platform provides an accessible route for students to fabricate, characterize, and analyze field-effect devices without access to conventional semiconductor foundry.
articles.summary_en: Researchers demonstrate a low-infrastructure method for fabricating and testing MoS₂ field-effect transistors using ionic-gel gating, off-the-shelf electrode arrays, and mechanically exfoliated flakes. The approach avoids cleanroom processing and vacuum deposition, making van der Waals transistor experiments accessible in teaching laboratories.

articles.title_original: Graphene-enabled electrically reconfigurable terahertz metasurface sensor
articles.title_en: Graphene Enables Electrically Reconfigurable Terahertz Metasurface Sensor
articles.excerpt_original: This study numerically demonstrates a graphene-enabled electrically reconfigurable terahertz metasurface sensor comprising asymmetric gold strips, a graphene monolayer, a SiO 2 spacer, and a gold back reflector. Within this fixed geometry, Fermi-level control selects overlapping calibration windows across refractive indices of 1.0–1.9, with peak absorptance of 97.21%–99.97% and sensitivities of 25.37–27.47 GHz RIU −1 . At unit refractive index, tuning the Fermi level from 0.4 to 0.9 eV shifts the resonance from 2.064 to 2.199 THz. A 60-state calibration surface, independently validated at eight off-grid states, yields a refractive-index inversion root-mean-square error of 0.0203 RIU. Electrical reconfiguration translates the sensing window and enables resonance placement within an instrumental band. At selected states, Q and FOM increase through linewidth narrowing even though the fitted sensitivity decreases.
articles.summary_en: Researchers numerically demonstrated a graphene-based terahertz metasurface sensor with electrically tunable resonance placement and refractive-index calibration. The design achieved up to 99.97% absorptance and a refractive-index inversion error of 0.0203 RIU across 60 calibration states.

articles.title_original: Washing-Engineered Graphene Aerogels: From Acid Etching to Electrolyte-Targeted Energy Storage Performance
articles.title_en: Washing Engineering Tunes Graphene Aerogels for Aqueous Supercapacitors
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract The porous structure and surface chemistry of graphene aerogels (GAs), critical to their energy storage performance in aqueous supercapacitors, can be effectively modulated by postoxidation washing treatments. In this study, three graphene aerogel samples, namely water-washed graphene aerogel (GA-W), acid–water cowashed graphene aerogel (GA-A/W), and acid-washed graphene aerogel (GA-A), were prepared through hydrothermal assembly of graphene oxide with different washing protocols. Experimental characterizations and density functional theory calculations confirm that residual protons trigger the transformation of carbonyl groups to hydroxyl moieties, accompanied by lattice distortion and pore collapse. Electrochemical measurements show that GA-W with a microporous structure and intact sp2 network achieves a specific capacitance of 319 F g–1 at 1 A g–1 in 6 M KOH electrolyte via dominant electric double-layer capacitance. Benefiting from high mesopore fraction (86.7%) and moderate carbonyl retention, GA-A/W delivers a capacitance of 248 F g–1 at 1 A g–1 in 0.5 M (NH4)2SO4 electrolyte, owing to matched ion transport channels and enhanced proton-coupled electron transfer (PCET) pseudocapacitance. This work elucidates the proton-induced structural degradation mechanism of GAs and proves that washing engineering is a facile and scalable approach to develop electrolyte-adaptive carbon electrodes for aqueous supercapacitors.
articles.summary_en: ACS researchers show that postoxidation washing controls graphene aerogel pore structure and surface chemistry, significantly affecting capacitance and electrolyte compatibility. Water-washed aerogels reached 319 F g−1 in KOH, while acid–water co-washed aerogels achieved 248 F g−1 in ammonium sulfate through enhanced proton-coupled charge storage.

articles.title_original: Optimized microstructure and enhanced multifunctional properties of Sn-25Bi solder alloys reinforced with exfoliated Ti3C2Tx MXene nanosheets
articles.title_en: MXene-Enhanced Sn-Bi Solder Improves Mechanical, Thermal and Electrical Performance
articles.excerpt_original: Purpose This study aims to examine the impact of Ti3C2Tx MXenes incorporation on the structural, mechanical, thermal, electrical and wettability characteristics of the Sn-25Bi binary solder alloy. Design/methodology/approach Sn-25Bi-mTi3C2Tx nanocomposite solder alloys (m = 0, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6 and 0.8 Wt.%) were developed by blending Sn and Bi powders with Ti3C2Tx MXene nanosheets. The mixtures were compacted into disc-shaped pellets using a 12 mm diameter steel die and a manual hydraulic press with a 5-tonne jack, which ensured uniform densification and adequate green strength. Findings The incorporation of 0.4 Wt. % of Ti3C2Tx significantly enhances Vickers microhardness (Hv) and elastic modulus (Y), achieving values of 40.5 MPa and 0.67 GPa, respectively, which corresponds to about a 97% increase compared to the Ti3C2Tx-free alloy. Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) indicated a decreased melting temperature of 194.99°C and a constricted mushy zone of ΔT = 11.29°C, implying enhanced thermal stability and consistent phase transition behavior at 0.4 Wt.%. Moreover, the solder’s wettability was improved, demonstrated by a minimum contact angle of 20.7° and a maximum spreading area of 0.773 cm2 at the identical composition. Electrical characterization demonstrated a substantial reduction in electrical resistivity (ρ) by approximately 35% and a notable increase in free electron concentration (N) and Fermi velocity (Vf). However, excessive MXene loading beyond 0.4 Wt.% resulted in agglomeration-induced performance degradation across all investigated properties. Research limitations/implications The results are confined to the Sn-25Bi/Ti3C2Tx formulations examined. Further microstructural examination is necessary to enhance comprehension of the distribution of MXene nanosh
articles.summary_en: Researchers optimized Sn-25Bi solder reinforced with Ti3C2Tx MXene nanosheets, identifying 0.4 wt.% as the best loading. This composition nearly doubled hardness and elastic modulus, improved wettability, lowered resistivity, and narrowed the mushy zone, while higher loadings caused agglomeration and performance losses.

articles.title_original: Exploring SnS2/graphene heterostructure as next-generation anode for rechargeable potassium-ion batteries
articles.title_en: SnS₂/Graphene Heterostructure Explored for Potassium-Ion Battery Anodes
articles.summary_en: Academic research examines a tin disulfide/graphene heterostructure as a potential anode material for rechargeable potassium-ion batteries. The study signals interest in graphene-enabled electrode architectures for emerging energy-storage chemistries.

articles.title_original: Frequency-Dependent Vibration Damping and Energy Dissipation in Monolayer and Bilayer Graphene: A Molecular Dynamics Study
articles.title_en: Molecular dynamics reveals frequency-dependent damping in monolayer and bilayer graphene
articles.excerpt_original: The vibration damping behavior of monolayer and bilayer graphene is investigated through molecular dynamics simulations, with particular emphasis on the effects of excitation frequency and interlayer interactions on mechanical energy dissipation. Graphene nanoplates with in-plane dimensions of approximately 200 Å × 200 Å are considered, with the bilayer system arranged in an AB-stacking configuration. Atomic interactions are described using a reactive force field (ReaxFF), enabling the dynamic response and associated energy dissipation to emerge directly from the underlying atomistic interactions without introducing phenomenological damping parameters. A localized harmonic out-of-plane displacement with an amplitude of 0.4 nm is applied to the central region of the graphene nanoplate at excitation frequencies of 0.001, 0.01, 0.1, and 1 THz. Energy dissipation is quantified directly from the area enclosed by the resulting reaction force–displacement hysteresis loops, providing an energy-based characterization of the equivalent damping response. The results reveal a strongly frequency-dependent damping response and a non-monotonic effect of the second graphene layer. At 1 THz, the equivalent damping ratio reaches approximately 47.4% for monolayer graphene and 24.0% for bilayer graphene, despite comparable absolute cycle-energy values, demonstrating that the normalized damping response is strongly influenced by the dynamic reference energy. Overall, the results show that interlayer coupling can substantially modify the frequency-dependent vibration and energy-dissipation response of graphene rather than producing a uniform increase in damping.
articles.summary_en: A molecular dynamics study finds that graphene’s vibration damping and energy dissipation vary strongly with excitation frequency. At 1 THz, monolayer graphene shows an approximately 47.4% equivalent damping ratio versus 24.0% for bilayer graphene, indicating that interlayer coupling does not uniformly enhance damping.

articles.title_original: Quantum coupling of topological junction states in armchair graphene nanoribbon structures
articles.title_en: Quantum Coupling of Topological States in Graphene Nanoribbon Junctions
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Connecting armchair graphene nanoribbons in series generates topological junction states at the interface when the topology class is not matched due to their difference in the width. The number of such states is investigated for the systems where multiple nanoribbon junctions are mutually coupled quantum-mechanically in two manners. (1) Nonidentical junctions are asymmetrically series-connected. (2) The nanoribbon structures contain parallel paths. It is shown for the asymmetric structures that unpaired states are present at the Dirac point in addition to the paired states that appear away from the Dirac point. The topology class is not established for the individual narrow-wide interfaces in the situation of the parallel paths. The total winding number that provides the number of the topological states is given for the whole junction hosting the parallel paths. Furthermore, the overlap of the topological zero-energy states when the above nanoribbon structures are repeated periodically as superlattices is found to produce no Bloch mode at the Dirac point.
articles.summary_en: Theoretical research examines how topological junction states couple in armchair graphene nanoribbon structures with asymmetric series connections and parallel paths. It finds unpaired Dirac-point states in asymmetric structures and no Bloch mode at the Dirac point in periodically repeated superlattices.

articles.title_original: Microwave spectroscopic evidence of a moiré-commensurate electron crystal in monolayer graphene
articles.title_en: Microwave spectroscopy reveals moiré-commensurate electron crystal in monolayer graphene
articles.excerpt_original: We probe the conductivity of the lowest Landau level of a moiré-aligned monolayer graphene device by broadband microwave transmission through a coplanar waveguide ($\sim$50 mK, 15.4--18 T), isolating the longitudinal channel through a low-minus-high frequency band difference $D(ν)$. We resolve a series of minima in $D(ν)$ that drift with field along lines of fixed carrier density rather than fixed Landau filling, the hallmark of moiré-commensurate electron crystals. The strongest minimum is present at every field and matches no fractional quantum Hall or integer Hofstadter state. It lies at band filling $s=1/3$, one electron for every three moiré cells---the generalized Wigner crystal that DaSilva, Jung, and MacDonald predict as the most favorable fixed-density ($t=0$) commensuration. The weaker minima fall near neighboring commensurate fillings.
articles.summary_en: Researchers used broadband microwave transmission at millikelvin temperatures and high magnetic fields to identify conductivity minima associated with fixed-density moiré commensurations. The strongest feature occurs at one electron per three moiré cells, consistent with a generalized Wigner crystal rather than conventional fractional quantum Hall or Hofstadter states.

articles.title_original: Hierarchically Engineered MXene/CMC‐Na Composites with Acetaminophen Modification for Self‐Powered Humidity Sensing
articles.title_en: Self-Powered MXene–CMC Composite Sensors Enable Humidity and Respiratory Monitoring
articles.excerpt_original: ABSTRACT Humidity sensors have demonstrated significant potential for applications in wearable electronics, physiological monitoring, and environmental sensing. However, the practical implementation of humidity sensors is often limited by reliance on external power sources, making the development of self‐powered humidity sensing systems a considerable challenge. This work presents a hierarchical multi‐step modification strategy to fabricate an acetaminophen (AP)‐modified hydroxylated MXene/carboxymethylcellulose sodium (CMC‐Na) hybrid gel ink (AHMC) with integrated humidity sensing and self‐powered functionality. Theoretical calculations reveal that AHMC exhibits exceptional water adsorption capacity, characterized by a lower adsorption energy (−0.42 eV) and a shorter adsorption distance (1.69 Å) compared to MXene. The screen‐printed paper‐based AHMC humidity sensor (PB‐AHMC) demonstrates a rapid capacitive response (4.8/0.6 s) and remarkable response (73524%) with excellent bending stability and environmental durability. Furthermore, the PB‐AHMC‐based humidity sensor array (PCSA) accurately identifies various subtle respiratory abnormalities with the incorporation of machine learning algorithms. Significantly, a self‐powered sensor (SP‐AHMC) driven by redox reactions has been developed, achieving a broad detection range (11%–97% RH), exhibiting minimal hysteresis (1.0% RH), and delivering a peak output voltage of 0.43 V at 97% RH. Collectively, the AHMC‐based sensors demonstrate substantial potential for advancing applications in healthcare monitoring, non‐contact humidity detection, and self‐powered systems.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed acetaminophen-modified MXene/carboxymethylcellulose sodium composite gel sensors with rapid response, broad humidity detection, and self-powered operation. Screen-printed arrays also identified subtle respiratory abnormalities using machine learning, supporting wearable and environmental sensing applications.

articles.title_original: Study on the regulation mechanism of hydration behavior, durability and electrochemical performance of Portland cement via nanocellulose-MXene synergistic modification
articles.title_en: Nanocellulose–MXene Modification Improves Conductive Concrete Durability
articles.excerpt_original: Cement-based materials face a fundamental contradiction, where achieving good structural load-bearing capacity, excellent conductivity, and long-term corrosion resistance remains challenging. However, how to introduce stable conductive phases and simultaneously improve strength without sacrificing durability remains a key scientific problem in functional concrete. To address this challenge, this study proposes a synergistic modification strategy using cellulose nanofibers (CNF) and MXene, systematically evaluating the multiscale effects of different dosages on hydration kinetics, pore structure, and electrochemical properties. The results show that only within a narrow range of CNF ≈ 20 mL and MXene ≈ 12 mL, the material can self-assemble a "high-speed electron channel – slow ion channel – interface passivation" triple barrier. MXene conductive nanosheets construct high-speed electron channels that lower the resistivity, while CNF regulates the formation of dense C-S-H gel networks that act as slow ion channels to retard corrosion ion diffusion. The synergistic modification also produces an enhanced interfacial protective effect, which may be associated with interactions among the surface functional groups of MXene/CNF and Ca²⁺ in the cementitious matrix. This synergistic mechanism contributes to a more favorable balance between electrical conductivity and corrosion resistance through coordinated regulation of electronic transport, ionic transport, and pore structure. This study provides a replicable nanostructure paradigm for marine concrete, 3D printing, and smart infrastructure, laying the foundation for the molecular-level design of green multifunctional concrete.
articles.summary_en: Researchers report that a narrow combination of cellulose nanofibers and MXene creates complementary electron-transport, ion-barrier, and interface-passivation effects in Portland cement. The approach may support conductive marine concrete, 3D-printed cement, and smart infrastructure, although the findings remain at the research stage.

articles.title_original: Computational screening of transition metal and sulfur Co-doped h-BN: Toward selective and active electrocatalysts for CO2 reduction
articles.title_en: Computational screening of sulfur- and transition-metal-doped h-BN electrocatalysts for CO₂ reduction
articles.summary_en: This academic study computationally screens hexagonal boron nitride co-doped with transition metals and sulfur for selective, active CO₂-reduction electrocatalysts. No experimental validation or performance results are provided in the available record.

articles.title_original: Selective etching of 2D materials for quantum computing devices: A computational perspective
articles.title_en: Computational Design of Selective Etching for Quantum-Grade 2D Devices
articles.excerpt_original: Achieving atomic-level precision in the fabrication of quantum devices built from two-dimensional (2D) materials requires a thorough understanding of how selective etching reshapes surface chemistry, defect populations, and electronic structure at the nanoscale. This review consolidates recent computational advances in density functional theory, molecular dynamics, machine learning, and quantum chemical methods that model etching pathways in graphene, transition metal dichalcogenides, hexagonal boron nitride, and MXenes. We critically assess how these simulations predict etchant–surface reactivity, defect-driven selectivity, and post-etch changes in band structure, spin–orbit coupling, valley polarization, and coherence lifetimes. Key experimental validations, including graphene Josephson junctions, etched double quantum dots, and MoS₂ valley qubits, illustrate how reliably simulations can guide fabrication. Closed-loop machine-learning–density-functional-theory frameworks and digital twin architectures are highlighted as promising routes toward automated, adaptive manufacturing of quantum-grade 2D devices. The review also identifies persistent gaps in multi-scale modelling and dynamic environment simulation, and suggests directions for future research.
articles.summary_en: A review examines computational methods for selectively etching graphene and other 2D materials, focusing on defect control, electronic structure, and quantum-device performance. It highlights machine-learning/DFT workflows and digital twins as potential tools for adaptive manufacturing, while noting persistent multiscale-modeling challenges.

articles.title_original: Graphene as a Tunable Nonradiative Bath for Moiré Excitons
articles.title_en: Graphene Enables Tunable Nonradiative Control of Moiré Excitons
articles.excerpt_original: A minimal theory of nonradiative energy transfer from a two-dimensional (2D) moiré exciton to a nearby graphene layer is presented. From Fermi’s golden rule the transfer rate is the overlap of the exciton near-field spectrum with the dissipative density response of graphene, weighted by an exciton form factor, and it reproduces the established Γ ET ∝ [Formula: see text] −4 law in the point-dipole limit. A finite exciton size filters out the high-momentum near field once the spacer thickness approaches the transition-polarization radius R X , so the distance dependence of the rate — and of the photoluminescence (PL) quenching — probes the exciton size. A low-momentum expansion shows that, relative to the calibrated point-dipole response of the same bath, this leading correction is set by R X alone. In the ideal coherent-envelope limit the accompanying giant oscillator strength makes the rate non-monotonic in the exciton size, with a peak near [Formula: see text]. Treating graphene as a gate-tunable bath, Pauli blocking suppresses the interband channel once 2|μ F | approaches ħω, partially restoring PL, and a full random-phase-approximation benchmark confirms the normalized interband distance dependence to within a few percent away from the threshold. Mapping the PL observables across the transition-metal dichalcogenide/hexagonal boron nitride/graphene parameter space, we find that a graphene gate acts not as a passive electrostatic element but as a tunable 2D electronic reservoir probed through exciton PL quenching.
articles.summary_en: A theoretical study models energy transfer from moiré excitons to nearby graphene and shows that exciton size can be inferred from distance-dependent photoluminescence quenching. Gate-tunable graphene modulates this transfer through Pauli blocking, positioning it as an active electronic reservoir for exciton-based optoelectronic systems.

articles.title_original: Transdimensional Chern insulators in rhombohedral multilayer graphene superlattices
articles.title_en: Theory predicts Chern insulator phases in multilayer graphene
articles.excerpt_original: Recent experiments on lightly electron-doped rhombohedral multilayer graphene (RMG) in the "transdimensional" regime revealed anomalous Hall hysteresis under both perpendicular and in-plane magnetic fields, pointing to the emergence of transdimensional orbital magnetism in an interaction-driven "Fermi-lune" metal. Here we demonstrate that, by coupling to the moiré potential, this transdimensional orbital ferromagnetic metal can evolve into quantized Chern insulator phases in twisted RMG/hBN moiré superlattices. Using unrestricted Hartree-Fock calculations, we find that interaction-driven reconstruction isolates a spin-valley-polarized $|C| = 1$ Chern band, leading to a "transdimensional Chern insulator" (TDCI) state exhibiting both in-plane and out-of-plane orbital magnetizations. A minimal two-band model is introduced to describe the unique properties of TDCI, which unveils the intimate connection between non-reciprocal velocity and in-plane orbital magnetization. We further analyze the collective excitations of TDCIs, and identify soft charge and spin modes that may lead to density wave instabilities in certain cases. An in-plane magnetic field can harden the soft density-wave mode and may drive a transition from density-wave state to TDCI. Finally, when the $|C| = 1$ band is fractionally filled, the many-body ground state may be a fractional Chern insulator with broken rotation and mirror symmetries.
articles.summary_en: Hartree–Fock calculations predict transdimensional Chern insulator states in twisted rhombohedral multilayer graphene/hBN moiré superlattices. The proposed phases exhibit coupled in-plane and out-of-plane orbital magnetization, with fractional Chern insulator states possible at partial band filling.

articles.title_original: Nonlinear flutter characteristics of graphene-reinforced porous folding wing-plate
articles.title_en: Graphene–Aluminum Folding Wings Show Improved Supersonic Flutter Stability
articles.excerpt_original: The flutter research on folding wings is of crucial engineering significance for ensuring structural safety, aeroelastic stability, and suppressing nonlinear vibration behaviors under supersonic flight conditions. Taking the physical prototype of Lockheed Martin's folding-wing unmanned aerial vehicle as the research object, this paper establishes the aerodynamic force according to the first-order piston theory. Considering three porosity distribution patterns and three graphene distribution types, the dynamic governing equations of the graphene nanoplatelet-reinforced porous aluminum matrix sandwich (GNPs-PFMSC) folding wing-plate are derived using the first-order shear deformation theory (FSDT) and von Kármán large deformation assumption. The effects are systematically investigated for the porosity distribution, graphene distribution type, porosity coefficient, graphene mass fraction, folding angle and yaw angle on the critical flutter aerodynamic pressure (CFAP) of the structure. Moreover, the vibration responses of the system before and after the CFAP, especially the limit cycle oscillation (LCO) behavior, are analyzed. It is found that X-type and X-pattern distributions exhibit higher CFAP and smaller limit cycle amplitudes, indicating superior stiffness distribution and stronger flutter suppression capability. Increasing the porosity reduces the CFAP and increases the flutter amplitude, while increasing the graphene mass fraction enhances the CFAP and effectively suppresses the amplitude. A larger yaw angle significantly increases the CFAP and suppresses the vibration amplitude; as the folding angle increases, the CFAP first increases and then decreases, making the folding angle a dominant factor affecting flutter stability. This study provides important theoretica
articles.summary_en: A modeling study finds that graphene nanoplatelet reinforcement can increase critical flutter pressure and suppress vibration in porous aluminum sandwich folding wing-plates. The results indicate potential relevance to supersonic UAV aeroelastic design, with graphene distribution, porosity, folding angle, and yaw angle strongly affecting stability.

articles.title_original: Mechanism of TiO₂ polymorph selection during Ti₃C₂Tₓ MXene oxidation
articles.title_en: Mechanism of TiO₂ Polymorph Selection During Ti₃C₂Tₓ MXene Oxidation
articles.summary_en: Academic research examines how oxidation drives TiO₂ polymorph selection in Ti₃C₂Tₓ MXene. The findings may inform control of MXene oxidation products and material performance.

articles.title_original: Intrinsic p-type Ohmic contacts in monolayer α-CNH: A strategy for overcoming the barriers challenge in 2D FETs
articles.title_en: Study proposes intrinsic p-type Ohmic contacts for α-CNH 2D FETs
articles.excerpt_original: Realizing low-barrier p-type contacts is crucial yet highly challenging for two-dimensional (2D) semiconductor devices. Herein, based on density functional theory, we propose a strategy that leverages the intrinsic properties of the 2D semiconductor to achieve low-barrier p-type Ohmic contacts without introducing additional process complexity. Interfacial interactions and electronic-structure alignment with the electrode material further influence the contact properties. Specifically, we use monolayer α-CNH—a novel 2D semiconductor with a direct bandgap and high carrier mobility—as the channel material. We systematically investigate the electronic properties of metal-CNH contacts. The results show that most three-dimensional (3D) metal-CNH contacts achieve p-type quasi-Ohmic or Ohmic behavior. Such p-type Ohmic contacts, enabled by the inherent material characteristics, effectively suppress the Schottky barrier without introducing an additional tunneling barrier. Moreover, compared to 2D metal-CNH contacts, the 3D metal-CNH contacts exhibit smaller tunneling barriers. Quantum transport simulations further indicate that most of the investigated p-type transistors based on 3D metal-CNH contacts exhibit no lateral Schottky barrier. The strategy for realizing p-type Ohmic contacts demonstrated in our work offers new insights into material selection and contact design for achieving high-performance p-type 2D FETs.
articles.summary_en: Density functional theory and quantum transport simulations indicate that many three-dimensional metal contacts can form p-type quasi-Ohmic or Ohmic interfaces with monolayer α-CNH. The approach suppresses Schottky barriers without additional tunneling layers, offering a route to improved contact design in 2D field-effect transistors.

articles.title_original: Graphene-Oxide-Reinforced Perfluorocyclobutyl Polymer Coatings for Tunable Tortuosity-Driven Corrosion Protection
articles.title_en: Graphene oxide improves PFCB coating corrosion resistance
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Polymeric coatings are widely used to mitigate corrosion by limiting the transport of water, oxygen, and aggressive ions, yet their long-term performance is often constrained by permeability, electrostatic heterogeneity, and mechanically induced defects. Perfluorocyclobutyl (PFCB) polymers offer intrinsically low permeability and high chemical stability, but opportunities remain to further engineer ion-transport pathways without sacrificing adhesion or durability. The role of two-dimensional nanofillers in fluoropolymer matrices and the limits at which they enhance rather than degrade corrosion resistance also remain poorly understood. Here, we examine how the dispersion state of graphene oxide (GO) in an elastomer-modified PFCB (EPFCB) network couples ion-transport resistance with the electrical response of the coating and buried interface. At 0.10 wt % GO, the coating sustains low-frequency electrochemical impedance values on the order of 109–1010 Ω·cm2 for over 30 days in 3.5 wt % NaCl solution, representing three orders of magnitude improvement over the neat EPFCB coating. This performance is supported by Raman-verified defect-rich GO, homogeneous platelet dispersion observed by electron microscopy, suppression of surface potential fluctuations by Kelvin probe force microscopy, and a controlled increase in glassy modulus from ∼218 MPa to ∼1.6–1.9 GPa without excessive brittleness. In contrast, higher GO loadings (>0.25 wt %) promote aggregation, greater morphological and electrostatic heterogeneity, earlier electrolyte breakthrough, and accelerated scribe creep during cyclic corrosion testing. These findings demonstrate that GO influences EPFCB performance through the combined effects of platelet-induced transport obstruction and dispersion-dependent ele
articles.summary_en: Researchers found that 0.10 wt% graphene oxide increased low-frequency impedance in elastomer-modified perfluorocyclobutyl coatings to 10⁹–10¹⁰ Ω·cm² for more than 30 days in saline exposure. Higher loadings caused aggregation, electrolyte breakthrough, and faster corrosion damage, highlighting a narrow formulation window for durable protective coatings.

articles.title_original: Surface diffusion strategies for chemical vapor deposition of 2D Nb2C MXene films
articles.title_en: Surface-diffusion CVD enables large-scale growth of bare Nb2C MXene films
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Chemical vapor deposition (CVD) is a thriving bottom-up synthesis technique that serves as an alternative to the conventional methods involving the etching of layered MAX phases. CVD is particularly advantageous in terms of large-scale synthesis and atomic economy, time and energy savings, as well as the capability to produce bare MXenes without surface terminations. However, its widespread employment remains limited as the growth generally only occurs in specific immiscible alloy systems consisting of transition metals (such as Mo) and low melting point catalytic metals (such as Cu). Here, we propose a surface diffusion liquid metal CVD (SDLM-CVD) method for synthesizing bare few-layer 2D Nb 2 C MXenes. Controlling the Nb/C ratio and its distribution on the Cu liquid surface is the key factor. Single crystalline bare Nb 2 C flakes with a trigonal structure were obtained in a specific region where the appropriate Nb/C ratio is satisfied. Additionally, a continuous 2D Nb 2 C film is formed by leveraging the self-assembling process that observed during the growth. The growth mechanism and the self-assembling mechanism were further elucidated through density functional theory calculations. The SDLM-CVD method provides a novel approach for the direct and large-scale synthesis of materials in the MXenes family.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a surface-diffusion liquid-metal CVD method to synthesize bare few-layer Nb2C MXene flakes and continuous films. The approach uses controlled niobium-to-carbon distribution on a liquid copper surface and could support scalable, termination-free MXene production.

articles.title_original: Stretchable h‐BN/TPU Fibers for Passive‐Active Dual‐Mode Thermal Management and Wearable Haptic Interfaces
articles.title_en: Stretchable h-BN/TPU Fibers Enable Dual-Mode Thermal Management and Wearable Haptics
articles.excerpt_original: ABSTRACT Wearable thermal interfaces require rapid, spatially confined thermal feedback together with mechanical compliance, yet existing passive thermal‐management textiles and active thermal‐haptic devices remain largely separate. Here, a stretchable h ‐BN/TPU composite fiber is developed by coupling microfluidic spinning with non‐solvent‐induced phase separation. Rectangular‐channel confinement aligns hexagonal boron nitride plates within a microporous thermoplastic polyurethane matrix, constructing directional heat‐conduction pathways while preserving large deformation. The optimized 30 wt.% h ‐BN/TPU fiber achieves a dry‐state thermal conductivity of 2.08 and 4.14 W·m −1 ·K −1 under humid conditions, together with 9.67 MPa tensile strength and 422% elongation at break. Pareto‐front analysis identifies the 30 wt.% composition as the thermal‐mechanical knee, arising from the coupled effects of filler orientation, low void fraction, and deformable TPU domains. Woven h ‐BN/TPU fabrics provide passive thermal management, reducing surface temperature by 5.7°C under simulated solar irradiation and maintaining performance after 2000 bending cycles. When integrated into a thermal feedback glove, the fabric enables localized fingertip actuation with a heating rate of +29.55°C·s −1 and a thermal relaxation time of ∼20 s (returning below the warm perception threshold of 35°C). This fiber platform bridges passive heat regulation and active thermal haptics for next‐generation thermally interactive wearables.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed stretchable hexagonal boron nitride/thermoplastic polyurethane composite fibers with directional heat conduction, high elongation, and durability after 2,000 bending cycles. Woven fabrics provided passive cooling and enabled localized thermal feedback in a glove, combining thermal management with wearable haptic actuation.

articles.title_original: Quasi-Ballistic Thermal Transport in Vertically Aligned h-BN
articles.title_en: Vertically Aligned h-BN Enables Quasi-Ballistic Heat Transport Below 400°C
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Hexagonal boron nitride (h-BN) has attracted significant interest in the semiconductor industry due to its wide bandgap (5.95 eV), high anisotropic thermal conductivity, and low dielectric constant. However, the formation of crystalline h-BN conventionally requires high processing temperatures, which are incompatible with back-end-of-line (BEOL) integration and advanced packaging processes that must remain below 400 °C to avoid degradation of front-end devices. In this work, trichloroborazine (TCB) was systematically investigated using ammonia as the nitrogen co-reactant under both plasma-enhanced atomic layer deposition (PEALD) and atomic layer annealing (ALA) conditions. In the ALA process, low-energy inert ions are shown to enable in situ crystallization at temperatures well below those required for conventional MOCVD. As a result, highly ordered, vertically aligned polycrystalline h-BN films were deposited within a BEOL-compatible temperature window of 300–400 °C. The as-deposited ALA h-BN films exhibited clear signatures of cross-plane quasi-ballistic phonon transport over a thickness range of 20–50 nm, characterized by a thickness-independent effective thermal resistance of ∼6–9 m2 K GW–1. This invariance with film thickness indicates that phonon mean free paths exceed the film thickness, confirming quasi-ballistic heat transport enabled by the high crystallinity and preferential vertical alignment of the h-BN domains.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed vertically aligned polycrystalline h-BN films using atomic layer annealing at 300–400°C, compatible with back-end-of-line semiconductor processing. Films 20–50 nm thick showed thickness-independent thermal resistance, indicating quasi-ballistic phonon transport enabled by high crystallinity and vertical alignment.

articles.title_original: Modular van der Waals MOSFETs through layer-by-layer chalcogen substitutions
articles.title_en: Layer-by-layer chalcogen substitution enables modular van der Waals MOSFETs
articles.excerpt_original: In two-dimensional transition-metal dichalcogenides (TMDCs), the local electrostatic field of the chalcogen p -orbitals dictates the crystal field splitting of the transition metal d -orbitals, stabilizing diverse electronic states from semiconducting and semimetallic to exotic topological phases. On-demand substitution of the lattice chalcogens is therefore an efficient route to tuning TMDC electronic phases. Here, we custom-molded van der Waals (vdW) heterostructures by layer-by-layer vapor-phase chalcogen substitution starting from p -type WSe 2 multilayers into which we locally inscribed insulating WO x , n -type WS 2 , and semimetallic WTe 2 . This spatially precise conversion seamlessly integrated distinct electronic phases, both vertically and laterally, into modular vdW semiconductor heterostructures that are otherwise inaccessible. As a demonstration, we integrated WO x /WSe 2 local gate stacks to build ultrascaled metal oxide–semiconductor field effect transistors (MOSFETs), achieving an unprecedented subthreshold swing at subnanometer equivalent oxide thickness.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a vapor-phase process that locally converts multilayer WSe2 into insulating WOx, n-type WS2, and semimetallic WTe2, integrating distinct electronic phases vertically and laterally. Demonstration devices using WOx/WSe2 gate stacks achieved a reported subthreshold swing at subnanometer equivalent oxide thickness, indicating potential for ultrascaled semiconductor devices.

articles.title_original: Zigzag graphene nanoribbons as a Majorana platform
articles.title_en: Zigzag graphene nanoribbons proposed as a tunable Majorana platform
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Graphene nanoribbons support a variety of electronic phases that can be tuned via external stimuli. In particular, zigzag graphene nanoribbons exhibit an antiferromagnetic insulating ground state which can transition to a half-metallic phase under a transverse electric field or when embedded in hexagonal boron nitride. Here, we develop a simple model of a heterostructure composed of a half-metallic zigzag graphene nanoribbon coupled with an Ising superconductor. We demonstrate that an Ising superconductor’s s -wave spin-singlet pairing gap component can induce a spin-triplet, odd-parity pairing gap in the half-metallic phase of the nanoribbon via proximity coupling. The resulting superconducting phase is topologically nontrivial, with gate-tunable transitions that enable the emergence of Majorana zero modes.
articles.summary_en: IOP Publishing research models a heterostructure combining a half-metallic zigzag graphene nanoribbon with an Ising superconductor. The model predicts gate-tunable topological superconductivity and the emergence of Majorana zero modes through proximity-induced spin-triplet pairing.

articles.title_original: Scalable assembly of MXene/ANF nanofluidic membranes induced by shear-flow-alignment for giant osmotic energy harvesting
articles.title_en: Shear-aligned MXene/ANF membranes enable high-density osmotic energy harvesting
articles.excerpt_original: Two-dimensional (2D) nanofluidic membranes have demonstrated extraordinary promise in high-throughput ionic transport systems for water-energy nexus applications. Nevertheless, the inability to engineer macroscopic, structurally ordered 2D membranes with precisely aligned nanochannels severely restricts their practical implementation. Here, we demonstrate a scalable shear-flow alignment strategy to assemble MXene/ANF composite membranes with vertically ordered nanochannels, which outperforms ionic flux leading to giant osmotic energy generation. The viscosity contrast between components generates sufficient shear-force gradients in dilute suspensions, enabling parallel alignment of MXene nanosheets during vacuum-assisted assembly. Under a 50-fold salinity gradient, the resulting vertically ordered architecture establishes ultralow-tortuosity ion highways, achieving unprecedented ionic flux (2.4 × 10 5 S/m 2 ) with near-perfect cation selectivity (0.94), leading to a power density of 81.8 W m −2 under a 500-fold concentration gradient (5 M/0.01 M NaCl). Remarkably, the MXene/ANF nanocomposite simultaneously achieves exceptional mechanical robustness (tensile strength: 348.9 MPa, Young's modulus: 19.9 GPa) and environmental stability (97.5% performance retention after 30-day operation). Theoretical simulations demonstrate that highly aligned channels can significantly reduce resistance and energy loss during ion transmembrane process. The combination of flow-directed assembly and nanoscale interface engineering presented here provides new insights into scalable fabrication of high-performance ion exchange membranes for sustainable energy applications.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a scalable shear-flow assembly method for MXene/aramid nanofiber membranes with vertically aligned nanochannels. The membranes delivered reported power density of 81.8 W m−2, high cation selectivity, mechanical strength, and 97.5% performance retention after 30 days.

articles.title_original: Dimensionality-Driven Charge Stabilization of Group-IV Color Centers in Diamond Ultrathin Films
articles.title_en: Dimensional confinement stabilizes quantum defects in diamane
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Neutral group-IV vacancy (XV, X = Si, Ge, Sn, and Pb) centers in diamond are promising solid-state spin-photon interfaces owing to favorable spin coherence and inversion-symmetry-protected optical transitions. However, stabilizing their neutral charge state typically requires stringent Fermi-level engineering in high-purity boron-doped diamond, which poses significant materials-growth challenges. Here, dimensional confinement in diamane offers an alternative for charge-state stabilization without intentional doping. Our results show that diamane thickness and surface chemical termination cooperatively tune the electronic structures of XV centers, while their neutral-state thermodynamic stability is enhanced. The zero-field splitting and spin–orbit coupling of XV centers could be tuned while largely preserving their optical transition energies. We find hydrogenated diamane offers the best balance between charge-state stability and magneto-optical performance. More broadly, our findings establish dimensional confinement as a general strategy for engineering the charge, optical, and spin properties of solid-state quantum defects.
articles.summary_en: Researchers report that diamane thickness and surface termination can stabilize neutral group-IV vacancy centers without intentional doping. Hydrogenated diamane provides the strongest balance of charge stability and magneto-optical performance, offering a potential route to engineered solid-state quantum interfaces.

articles.title_original: Nodal nematic superconductivity in moiré graphene
articles.title_en: Moiré graphene exhibits nodal nematic superconductivity
articles.excerpt_original: Unconventional superconductivity can emerge in various forms in strongly correlated systems. Historically, the most extensively studied examples include nodal and triplet pairing, which were experimentally detected in cuprates and superfluid helium-3, respectively. Beyond these canonical cases, there are also nematic superconductors, in which the rotational symmetry of the lattice is broken in the superconducting state. While there are several examples of nematic superconductors whose pairing emerges inside a preexisting nematic normal state, experimental evidence for superconducting states that intrinsically break rotational symmetry on their own has been exceedingly scarce. Here, we report the experimental realization and identification of an intrinsic multi-component nodal nematic superconducting state in magic-angle twisted trilayer graphene (MATTG). By integrating tunneling spectroscopy with quantum transport measurements, we directly probe the symmetry of low-energy superconducting quasiparticles. Deep inside the superconducting state, we observe a pronounced two-fold anisotropy in the zero-bias tunneling conductance under an in-plane magnetic field, which is strongly suppressed together with superconductivity as the temperature or perpendicular magnetic field is increased. Remarkably, the major axis of anisotropy rotates by up to $90^{\circ}$ across the superconducting dome, indicating an intrinsic, field- and density-tunable symmetry of the low-energy excitations. These behaviors imply a nodal superconducting state in MATTG that spontaneously breaks the six-fold rotational symmetry of the moiré superlattice. Our results establish moiré graphene as a versatile platform for realizing and interrogating nodal nematic superconductivity, opening a new avenue for explo
articles.summary_en: Researchers report an intrinsic, multi-component nodal nematic superconducting state in magic-angle twisted trilayer graphene. Tunneling spectroscopy and quantum transport measurements revealed tunable two-fold anisotropy, establishing moiré graphene as a platform for studying unconventional superconductivity.

articles.title_original: Surface defects in anatase TiO₂ on graphene for LPG sensing: From molecular adsorption to electrical response
articles.title_en: Defect-engineered graphene–TiO₂ hybrid improves LPG sensing
articles.excerpt_original: The reliable detection of liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) is essential for safety in domestic and industrial environments due to its high flammability and the risks of accidental leakage. However, the role of specific surface defects in graphene-supported TiO₂ sensing materials remains poorly understood. Here, we combine density functional theory (DFT) with experimental characterization to investigate surface defects in a graphene–TiO₂ (GR–TiO₂) hybrid architecture for LPG sensing. At the atomic scale, oxygen vacancies and step-edge configurations on anatase TiO₂(101) modify the adsorption behavior of representative LPG components: methanethiol exhibits the most favorable interaction, particularly at under-coordinated and oxygen-deficient Ti sites, whereas propane and butane interact predominantly through weaker dispersion-driven contributions. These results identify surface coordination and oxygen deficiency as key factors governing molecular adsorption. Experimentally, a ~10 nm TiO₂ coating was deposited on hydroxylated graphene by atomic layer deposition. XPS revealed predominantly Ti⁴⁺ together with a Ti³ ⁺ contribution associated with locally reduced Ti environments, providing complementary evidence of oxygen-deficient TiO₂ consistent with the defect-related cathodoluminescence emission, while XRD confirmed that the employed ALD growth conditions produced the anatase TiO₂ phase. Under LPG exposure, the GR–TiO₂ device showed normalized current suppressions of ~97% and ~90% at + 3 V over two sequential exposures, with ~89% of the exposure-induced change recovered after a fixed 60 s interval. By linking defect-dependent adsorption to the measured electrical response, this study provides molecular-level insight into surface-defect engineering for GR-TiO₂ LPG sensors.
articles.summary_en: Researchers combined density functional theory with experiments to show that oxygen vacancies and step edges in anatase TiO₂ govern LPG adsorption on graphene-supported sensors. The device delivered approximately 97% and 90% current suppression during sequential exposures, with about 89% recovery after 60 seconds, highlighting defect engineering as a route to improved gas-sensor performance.

articles.title_original: Transport in multilayer graphene: resistance from stacking faults
articles.title_en: Stacking faults drive insulating behavior in multilayer graphene
articles.excerpt_original: Multilayer graphene exhibits rich possibilities for stacking. While natural bulk graphite predominantly occurs in the Bernal structure, where layers are stacked in an $-ABAB-$ pattern, rhombohedral stacking has sprung to prominence recently. It is well known that Bernal graphite exhibits anisotropic transport, with high resistance to currents along the stacking axis. Careful experiments using pillar geometries have measured out-of-plane resistance, attributing it to stacking faults where planes slip out of the nominal $ABAB$ sequence. The observed resistance shows anomalously large, non-Gaussian, sample-to-sample variations. In this article, we build a theoretical framework to calculate $c$-axis resistance of graphene stacks with an arbitrary stacking arrangement. Our approach builds on the idea that, regardless of stacking sequence, we have in-plane translational symmetry. With in-plane momentum as a good quantum number, $c$-axis transport reduces to an effectively one-dimensional problem that can be addressed using the Landauer paradigm. We calculate the resistances of a variety of simple stacking faults in both Bernal and rhombohedral systems. We also calculate the resistance of a rhombohedral 'slab' embedded between Bernal leads. Remarkably, despite both Bernal and rhombohedral graphite being metallic, the system exhibits insulating behaviour. We attribute this to Fermi surface mismatch. We next calculate the resistance of a multilayer sample with stacking disorder. Resistance is non-self-averaging, akin to a one-dimensional wire where disorder has a strong localizing effect. The median resistance grows exponentially with stack size, indicating insulating character driven by localization. Our results demonstrate that transport measurements on mesoscopic graphitic pi
articles.summary_en: A theoretical study finds that stacking faults and disorder can produce large, non-self-averaging out-of-plane resistance in multilayer graphene. Fermi-surface mismatch and localization cause resistance to rise exponentially with stack thickness, informing multilayer graphene transport and device design.

articles.title_original: Recent advances and emerging mechanisms in graphene-based materials for cartilage tissue engineering
articles.title_en: Graphene-Based Materials Advance Cartilage Tissue Engineering

This review synthesizes recent advances in graphene derivatives, scaffold fabrication strategies, and emerging mechanisms governing cell-graphene interactions. We evaluate how graphene enhances mechanical reinforcement, bioactivity, and matrix production across hydrogels, polymer composites, and ECM-derived scaffolds. Key opportunities and translational pathways are identified to guide the development of next-generation cartilage regeneration technologies.
