articles.title_original: Tunable Nonlinear Landscapes in Graphene Nanoelectromechanical Systems
articles.title_en: Graphene Resonator Enables Tunable Nonlinear Signal Processing
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Nonlinear nanomechanical resonators give convenient solid-state access to classical analogs of extreme nonlinear optics and to phononic signal processing. Here we report integer harmonic generation, phononic frequency sideband comb, and reverse period-doubling dynamics in a single platform of a suspended graphene resonator. A gate voltage breaks the out-of-plane symmetry of the membrane and establishes a 1:2 internal resonance between mechanical resonators. Under a single drive tone, integer harmonics are generated sequentially, forming a dense sideband frequency comb at larger drive. Raising the drive further, we find a reverse period-doubling transition: the comb spacing doubles, the line density halves, and energy flows back into the even-order comb lines. The measured spectrum yields the quadratic (ζ) and cubic (β) nonlinear coefficients of the membrane. These results demonstrate electrical control of several nonlinear landscapes in a single graphene resonator, enabling frequency multiplication, sideband comb generation, and broadband irregular motion.
articles.summary_en: Researchers demonstrate harmonic generation, frequency-comb formation, and reverse period-doubling in a suspended graphene nanoelectromechanical resonator. Gate-voltage control enables frequency multiplication and broadband nonlinear dynamics, supporting potential phononic signal-processing applications.

articles.title_original: Orbitronics in Zero-dimensional Graphene Nanoflakes via Electrode Coupling
articles.title_en: Graphene Nanoflakes Enable Zero-Dimensional Orbitronics
articles.excerpt_original: We show that graphene nanoflakes realize a previously unexplored form of orbitronics in which orbital currents emerge in the absence of intrinsic angular momentum of the constituent atoms. Starting with a hexagonal graphene nanoflake, we demonstrate the presence of energy-degenerate eigenstates with opposite non-zero expectation values of the angular momentum. Placing electrodes in an appropriate configuration on the flake couples the reservoirs more strongly to one of the two opposite-angular-momentum states, yielding a chiral current that carries a net orbital angular momentum. The resulting circulating orbital currents generate magnetic fringe fields that are experimentally accessible with spin centers or superconducting quantum interference magnetometers, providing avenues for their experimental realization. Finally, our work establishes a new platform for exploring and studying orbitronics in zero-dimensional systems.
articles.summary_en: Researchers show that electrode-coupled graphene nanoflakes can generate chiral currents carrying net orbital angular momentum without intrinsic atomic angular momentum. The resulting magnetic fringe fields could support experimental orbitronics studies using spin centers or superconducting quantum interference magnetometers.

articles.title_original: MXene-Based Flexible Piezoresistive Sensor for Non-Invasive Blood Pressure Monitoring
articles.title_en: MXene Flexible Sensor for Non-Invasive Blood Pressure Monitoring
articles.summary_en: Researchers report an MXene-based flexible piezoresistive sensor aimed at non-invasive blood pressure monitoring. The work combines flexible sensing with a biomedical monitoring application, although the available source provides no performance or validation details.

articles.title_original: Identification of carbon-related color centers in hBN by high-resolution ab initio photoluminescence modeling
articles.title_en: Ab initio modeling identifies carbon-related color centers in hBN
articles.excerpt_original: Identification of optically active defects in hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) remains challenging because different defect candidates can produce similar calculated photoluminescence (PL) lineshapes. Here, we demonstrate that force-constant embedding methodology can be extended to calculate high-resolution, vibrationally resolved PL lineshapes in the polar layered material hBN. Benchmarking against the carbon dimer defect, responsible for the 4.1 eV emission, we show that the methodology accurately reproduces the low-energy acoustic phonons and fine spectral features that are inaccessible when using direct supercell calculations. Applying the methodology to neutral carbon trimers ($\mathrm{C_2 C_B}$ and $\mathrm{C_2 C_N}$), we find that the calculated PL lineshape and excitation energy of $\mathrm{C_2 C_N}$ closely match the low-temperature spectrum of the emitter with a zero-phonon line at 1.54 eV. These results establish high-resolution phonon-sideband modeling as a powerful tool for discriminating among candidate defects in polar materials.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed high-resolution photoluminescence modeling to distinguish carbon-related defects in hexagonal boron nitride. Calculations matched a 1.54 eV emitter spectrum, supporting assignment to a neutral carbon trimer defect.

articles.title_original: AI-ready design of realistic 2D materials and interfaces with Mat3ra-2D
articles.title_en: Mat3ra-2D enables AI-ready modeling of realistic 2D materials
articles.excerpt_original: Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) models in materials science are predominantly trained on ideal bulk crystals, limiting their transferability to real-world applications where surfaces, interfaces, and defects dominate. We present Mat3ra-2D, an open-source framework for the rapid design of realistic two-dimensional materials and related structures, including slabs and heterogeneous interfaces, with support for disorder and defect-driven complexity. The approach combines: (1) well-defined standards for storing and exchanging materials data with a modular implementation of core concepts and (2) transformation workflows expressed as configuration-builder pipelines that preserve provenance and metadata. We implement typical structure generation tasks, such as constructing orientation-specific slabs or strain-matching interfaces, in reusable Jupyter notebooks that serve as both interactive documentation and templates for reproducible runs. To lower the barrier to adoption, we design the examples to run in any web browser and demonstrate how to incorporate these developments into a web application. Mat3ra-2D enables systematic creation, provenance tracking, inspection, and reuse of realistic 2D- and interface-aware structures, providing the structure-generation layer needed for future AI/ML dataset construction for training.
articles.summary_en: Researchers introduce Mat3ra-2D, an open-source framework for generating realistic two-dimensional materials, slabs, and heterogeneous interfaces incorporating defects, disorder, and strain. Its provenance-aware workflows could improve the reliability and reproducibility of future AI/ML materials datasets beyond idealized crystal models.

articles.title_original: Switchable altermagnetism and Luttinger-compensated ferrimagnetism in graphene-MnPS3 heterostructures
articles.title_en: Graphene–MnPS₃ Heterostructure Enables Switchable Compensated Magnetism
articles.excerpt_original: Altermagnetism (AM) and Luttinger-compensated ferrimagnetism (LC-FiM) both combine zero net magnetization with spin-split electronic bands, but realizing both states and their interconversion within a single platform remains a significant challenge. Using first-principles calculations and symmetry analysis, we show that a graphene-MnPS 3 van der Waals (vdW) heterostructure provides exactly such a platform. The graphene layer breaks the \({{\mathcal{P}}}{{\mathcal{T}}}\) symmetry of Néel-antiferromagnetic MnPS 3 , and the interfacial stacking dictates the symmetry relation between the two spin sublattices: hollow stacking preserves joint rotation and mirror operations, yielding an i -wave AM state with momentum-dependent spin splitting, while top stacking removes all sublattice-connecting symmetries and stabilizes an LC-FiM state with globally spin-split bands. The two phases are separated by an ultralow sliding barrier of 28 meV/f.u., allowing reversible switching by interlayer translation alone. Out-of-plane (OOP) pressure further amplifies the exchange spin splitting to 72.2 meV (AM) and 80.2 meV (LC-FiM), arising from strengthened interfacial coupling accompanied by enhanced orbital hybridization and asymmetric built-in polarization. Beyond the ideal-stacking limit, the intrinsic lattice mismatch generates a moiré superlattice of alternating AM and LC-FiM domains with distinct magneto-optical Kerr signatures. These results establish interfacial symmetry engineering as a general route to programmable compensated magnetism in vdW materials.
articles.summary_en: First-principles calculations identify graphene–MnPS₃ as a platform for switching between altermagnetic and Luttinger-compensated ferrimagnetic states through interlayer sliding. The predicted low switching barrier and pressure-enhanced spin splitting suggest potential for programmable spintronic and magneto-optical devices.

articles.title_original: High-performance p-type two-dimensional transistors enabled by weak disorder engineering
articles.title_en: Weak disorder engineering enables high-performance p-type 2D transistors
articles.excerpt_original: High-performance field effect transistors (FETs) demand efficient charge doping alongside superior charge transport, which has proven challenging for p-type two-dimensional (2D) semiconductors. Conventional substitutional impurity doping often induces severe lattice damage and deep-level acceptor states within 2D semiconductors, severely deteriorating carrier transport. Here, we demonstrate weak disorder engineering (WD)—a mild two-step procedure involving sulfur vacancy creation and subsequent oxygen passivation—to simultaneously achieve efficient hole doping and exceptional hole transport in 2D semiconductors (e.g., MoS2 and WS2, collectively denoted as MS2). First-principles calculations reveal that oxygen-passivated sulfur vacancies suppress deep trap states while preserving near-valence-edge occupied states (NVOS), rationalizing the simultaneous hole doping and high hole mobility. Photoelectron spectroscopy indicates the Fermi level (EF) of WD-MS2 is shifted by ~ 240 meV toward the valence band. Structural and Raman characterizations show that the mild process preserves the lattice integrity of 2D semiconductors and introduces compressive strain. Owing to NVOS‑induced efficient hole doping, suppressed deep‑trap states, preserved lattice integrity, and engineered compressive strain, the p‑type 2D WD‑MS2 FETs deliver high hole mobilities, high on/off ratios, and large current densities. Furthermore, high‑gain, low‑power 2D Complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor (CMOS) inverters are constructed by integrating p‑type WD-WS2 FETs. Stable p-type doping of 2D semiconductors remains an important challenge towards the development of complementary 2D electronics. Here, the authors report a procedure involving sulphur vacancy creation and subsequent oxygen passivation to rea
articles.summary_en: Researchers report a two-step sulfur-vacancy creation and oxygen-passivation process that provides p-type doping in MoS2 and WS2 while limiting lattice damage and deep traps. The resulting transistors show high hole mobility, strong switching performance, and enable high-gain, low-power 2D CMOS inverters.

articles.title_original: Graphene-confined growth of few-layer PtSe2 via one-step selenization
articles.title_en: Graphene-Confined Growth of Few-Layer PtSe₂ Demonstrated
articles.summary_en: Academic research reports a one-step selenization method for growing few-layer platinum diselenide (PtSe₂) within graphene-confined structures. The work is relevant to scalable synthesis of two-dimensional materials for semiconductor applications, although no device performance or commercial implications are provided.

articles.title_original: Decoupling the Conductivity–Seebeck Trade‐Off in N‐Type MXene/Conjugated Polyelectrolyte Thermoelectric Bilayers
articles.title_en: MXene–Polymer Bilayers Improve N-Type Thermoelectric Performance
articles.excerpt_original: ABSTRACT To decouple the Seebeck coefficient from electrical conductivity in metallic thermoelectric (TE) systems, we investigated bilayer heterostructures of MXene (Ti 3 C 2 T x ) and conjugated polymers with anionic (–SO 3– Na + , CPE‐Na), neutral (CP), and cationic (–N + (CH 3 ) 3 Br–, CPE‐Br) side chains. Strong electrostatic anchoring between the cationic ammonium side chains and electronegative MXene terminations induces a previously unreported Coulombic trap‐induced filtering mechanism, distinct from conventional energy filtering. The resulting localized potential wells selectively trap low‐energy carriers to enhance the Seebeck coefficient, while concurrent lattice stiffening suppresses electron–phonon scattering and preserves high‐energy carrier transport. This decoupling raises Hall mobility from 1.01 to 5.40 cm 2 V −1 s −1 and the Seebeck coefficient from –8.6 to –19.0 µV K −1 while maintaining a metallic conductivity of 5291.9 S cm −1 . The optimized MXene/CPE‐Br film, processed with a halogen‐free solvent, achieves a record power factor of 190.5 µW m −1 K −2 and a peak figure of merit ( zT ) of 0.0279. Strong interfacial adhesion further imparts good electromechanical durability under repeated bending to a flexible TE generator, providing an effective strategy to address the transport limitations of n‐type MXene‐based TE materials.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed MXene/conjugated-polyelectrolyte bilayers that decouple electrical conductivity and Seebeck coefficient through Coulombic carrier filtering. The optimized flexible film achieved a power factor of 190.5 µW m−1 K−2 and a peak zT of 0.0279 while maintaining bending durability.

articles.title_original: Sorption Molecular Dynamics of Point Defects in 2D Materials with a Machine Learning Potential
articles.title_en: Machine-learning molecular dynamics accelerates 2D-material defect screening
articles.excerpt_original: Defect engineering is a crucial tool for tuning and tailoring the properties of two-dimensional (2D) materials. A key challenge is identifying which defects are kinetically stable at room temperature and sufficiently promising to warrant further investigation. However, identifying stable defects with suitable properties using first-principles calculations, such as density functional theory (DFT) is computationally demanding, effectively limiting the scope of high-throughput studies. In this work, we investigate whether the machine learning interatomic potential MACE can reproduce sorption trends (adsorption vs. absorption) previously obtained from high-throughput DFT calculations and extend the analysis to elevated temperatures. A total of 17,624 defect structures from the ADAQ database are simulated using MACE-accelerated molecular dynamics (MD) at both 0 K and 300 K. The results show that MACE successfully reproduces the overall sorption trends observed in DFT calculations at 0 K at a fraction of the computational cost. Simulations performed at 300 K further indicate that the qualitative sorption trends remain largely the same when including finite-temperature effects. These findings demonstrate that MACE-driven MD can be used as an effective high-throughput prescreening tool for defect-related studies in 2D materials, specially related to sorption. While conventional first-principles methods, such as DFT, remain necessary for accurate and quantitative validation, the use of MLIPs enables MD simulations of finite-temperature defect behavior at a fraction of the computational cost of DFT-based MD.
articles.summary_en: Researchers used the MACE machine-learning potential to simulate 17,624 point-defect structures and reproduce DFT sorption trends at substantially lower computational cost. The results support high-throughput prescreening of finite-temperature defect behavior, while DFT remains necessary for quantitative validation.

articles.title_original: Plasmonic Monolayer MoS 2 for Ultrathin Photoelectrodes in Neutral Water
articles.title_en: Plasmonic Monolayer MoS₂ Enables Stable Neutral-Water Photoelectrodes
articles.excerpt_original: Photoelectrochemical (PEC) electrodes can be used to create hydrogen to sustainably generate low-cost fuel and produce petrochemical feedstock. However, most semiconductors that drive the aqueous redox reactions in PEC devices cannot survive in neutral water, critical for widescale commercial production. Emerging, two-dimensional monolayer semiconductors can be electrochemically stable but generally do not capture enough sunlight to produce effective amounts of hydrogen. In this work, we propose a new PEC architecture that uses plasmonic enhancement to increase photocurrent in a monolayer MoS 2 photocathode. By creating the first ZrN-based surface plasmon polariton (SPP) generator, we show fabricated nanostructures that plasmonically couple light with energies up to ~2.5 eV in water with near-100% light absorption. With transferred monolayer MoS 2 , the resulting Schottky diode demonstrates corrosion-free, fully stable photoactivity under 1-sun illumination in oxygenated, neutral water. We investigated and optimized the mechanisms of plasmonic enhancement, increasing photocurrent by up to 2.7x under AM1.5G illumination and 660% with wavelengths above the bandgap of monolayer MoS 2 . Furthermore, we show this architecture is compatible with standard roll-to-roll fabrication, and we use a technoeconomic analysis to estimate that levelized costs of hydrogen <$1/kg can be reasonably achieved with solar-to-hydrogen (STH) efficiencies of only 3.4%. Thus, with commercially scalable operational lifetimes and fabrication techniques, these results open the door to a new class of ultrathin PEC electrodes for economically feasible neutral water splitting applications.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a zirconium nitride plasmonic architecture that enhances monolayer MoS₂ photocathode performance in neutral water, increasing photocurrent by up to 2.7× under simulated sunlight. The study reports corrosion-free operation, roll-to-roll fabrication compatibility, and modeled hydrogen costs below $1/kg at 3.4% solar-to-hydrogen efficiency.

articles.title_original: Landscaping dual-ion batteries architected by MXene materials - Nature
articles.title_en: Review outlines MXene-based dual-ion batteries for low-temperature storage
articles.excerpt_original: Low-temperature rechargeable batteries are crucial for energy storage under subzero conditions but remain limited by sluggish ion transport, severe interfacial polarization, and slow charge-transfer kinetics. Dual-ion batteries (DIBs), employing both cations and anions as charge carriers, offer fast ion-storage kinetics and reduced desolvation barriers, yet practical applications are hindered by sluggish dual-ion diffusion, electrolyte incompatibility, and poorly understood interfacial processes. MXene materials, owing to their layered architectures, chemically tunable surfaces, and adjustable interlayer environments, all of which favor efficient ion storage and transport, are listed as electrode candidates, but suffer from nanosheet restacking, structural instability, and unresolved dual-ion storage mechanisms. This review identifies fundamental scientific questions governing low-temperature MXene-based DIBs and presents a unified mechanistic framework linking MXene chemistry, electrolyte properties, interfacial evolution, and dual-ion storage behavior. Critical challenges, materials-electrolyte-interface co-design strategies, and future research directions are highlighted to advance next-generation low-temperature DIBs.
articles.summary_en: A Nature review examines MXene materials as electrode candidates for low-temperature dual-ion batteries, focusing on ion transport, electrolyte compatibility and interfacial behavior. It proposes co-design strategies to address nanosheet restacking, structural instability and slow charge transfer.

articles.title_original: Direct view of exciton and carrier dynamics in twisted bilayer graphene
articles.title_en: Study directly observes exciton and carrier dynamics in twisted bilayer graphene
articles.excerpt_original: Twisted bilayer graphene (tBLG) on H-intercalated SiC (twist angle of $9 \pm 1^{\circ}$) is studied by position\mbox{-}, time\mbox{-}, and angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES). Both graphene layers are hole doped, with a Dirac-point offset of 30~meV. Time-resolved ARPES near the van Hove singularity reveals a spectral feature within the hybridization-induced band gap, together with excited electrons in the conduction band. The in-gap feature exhibits distinct dynamics, and its binding energy and $k$-space location are consistent with the proposed non-hydrogenic ``ghost-Fano'' exciton arising from destructive interference between two nearly degenerate excitonic channels. Near the Dirac points, the twist separates the largely layer-polarized Dirac cones in momentum space, providing direct layer selectivity. We find markedly different peak electronic temperatures in the two graphene layers, even though their subsequent cooling dynamics are very similar. We attribute this to an ultrafast interlayer redistribution of electronic energy, driven by an interlayer electric field that arises from the different doping in the layers.
articles.summary_en: Researchers used time-, position-, and angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy to observe a proposed ghost-Fano exciton and layer-selective electronic dynamics in twisted bilayer graphene. The findings reveal differing electronic temperatures between layers and ultrafast interlayer energy redistribution, informing fundamental understanding of graphene-based electronic systems.

articles.title_original: Phonon-Mediated Superconductivity near Phase Boundaries in Rhombohedral Multilayer Graphene
articles.title_en: Study models phonon-mediated superconductivity in rhombohedral multilayer graphene
articles.excerpt_original: The recent observation of superconductivity in untwisted multilayer graphene has sparked intense interest in its microscopic origin. As the displacement field and carrier density are varied, superconductivity emerges in several distinct regions with different temperature and magnetic-field responses. This behavior has been attributed to the presence of distinct electronic phases, raising the possibility that different superconducting regions originate from different microscopic mechanisms. While purely electronic pairing mechanisms have been extensively explored, an in-depth examination of phonon-mediated superconductivity is still missing. Here, we solve the coupled selfconsistent Migdal-Eliashberg equations using input from first-principles calculations and incorporating interaction-driven symmetry breaking of the electronic ground state. Varying the carrier density and displacement field, we reproduce the experimentally observed superconducting regions with comparable superconducting properties such as gap and $T_c$ and predict additional, as-yet undiscovered superconducting phases. Our findings exemplify that several superconductivity regions in rhombohedral graphene can be satisfactorily explained by phonon-mediated pairing.
articles.summary_en: Researchers used first-principles calculations and self-consistent Migdal–Eliashberg equations to reproduce observed superconducting regions in rhombohedral multilayer graphene. The work also predicts additional superconducting phases, supporting phonon-mediated pairing as an explanation for the material’s superconductivity.

articles.title_original: MXene Electrocatalysts for Selective Nitrogen Reduction Reaction‐to‐Ammonia Production: Surface Chemistry, Electronic Framework, and Design Principles
articles.title_en: Review outlines MXene design principles for selective ammonia electrocatalysis
articles.excerpt_original: ABSTRACT The electrochemical nitrogen reduction reaction (eNRR) is considered a promising approach to sustainable ammonia production compared with the Haber–Bosch process. However, eNRR remains significantly hindered by the extreme stability of the N≡N bond, slow proton‐coupled electron transfer (PCET), and the kinetically favored hydrogen evolution reaction (HER), which collectively reduce ammonia yield and Faradaic efficiency. MXenes represent a unique class of 2D transition‐metal carbides, nitrides, and carbonitrides, distinguished by chemically versatile transition‐metal active sites, defect‐rich structures, tunable surface terminations, and metallic conductivity. These properties enable unprecedented tuning of N 2 adsorption, interfacial charge redistribution, orbital hybridization, and adsorption energetics, enabling selective N 2 activation while minimizing competing proton reduction. This review provides a critical overview of the design principles of MXene‐based electrocatalysts for selective ammonia synthesis. The distinctive contribution of this review is to systematically link MXene composition, vacancy engineering, heteroatom doping, single‐atom anchoring, and assembling MXene heterostructures to their effects on electronic structure, adsorption free‐energy landscapes, NRR pathways, and HER suppression. Particular emphasis is placed on understanding catalytic selectivity in terms of the underlying mechanism and structure–activity relationships, derived through advanced operando characterization, density functional theory, and emerging machine‐learning‐assisted catalyst discovery.
articles.summary_en: The review examines how MXene composition, defects, surface terminations, heteroatom doping, single-atom anchoring, and heterostructures can improve electrochemical nitrogen reduction to ammonia. It links these features to nitrogen activation, suppression of competing hydrogen evolution, and catalyst discovery using operando characterization, density-functional theory, and machine learning.

articles.title_en: Redox Aqueous Electrolytes Enhance Titanium Carbide MXene Supercapacitors

Their overall electrochemical performance, however, strongly depends on the compatibility between the electrode active material and the electrolyte. This thesis presents the synthesis of Ti3C2Tx and investigates its electrochemical performance in redox coupled acidic and neutral aqueous electrolytes. articles.title_original: Confining Light in Hexagonal Boron Nitride Photonic Resonators
articles.title_en: Hexagonal Boron Nitride Resonators Demonstrate Tunable Quasi-BIC Photonics
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract van der Waals (vdWs) materials have been highly regarded in optoelectronics and nanophotonics, given that they exfoliate effortlessly and offer precise control over light–matter interactions. When constructed as metasurfaces, all-dielectric vdWs are capable of hosting tailored Mie responses across the visible-NIR spectra. However, typically Mie resonances are associated with low quality factors due to the inverse correlation between refractive index and bandgap energy. Here we demonstrate the existence of quasi-bound states in the continuum (qBIC) in a square array of tapered cylindrical resonators in the vdW hexagonal boron nitride. The mode frequency and quality factor are shown to be substantially modified by introducing vertical dielectric symmetry after coating the resonator array with PMMA. Our experimental study is supported by extensive optical simulations of transmittance for different structure parameters and environments. The agreement between theory and experiment is excellent. Our results confirm the potential of using qBICs in low-index materials with controllable features.
articles.summary_en: Researchers demonstrated quasi-bound states in the continuum (qBICs) in tapered hexagonal boron nitride photonic resonators. PMMA coating substantially modified the mode frequency and quality factor, highlighting potential for tunable low-index nanophotonic devices.

articles.title_original: Comparative investigation of chirality-dependent thermoelectric performance in hexagonal boron nitride nanoscrolls under ballistic transport regime
articles.title_en: Chirality Tunes Thermoelectric Performance of Boron Nitride Nanoscrolls
articles.excerpt_original: The ballistic thermoelectric performance of zigzag hexagonal boron nitride nanoscrolls (h-BNNSs) was systematically investigated for chiralities from (15,0) to (19,0) over 200–700 K using a tight-binding model and the Landauer–Büttiker formalism. All scrolls possess wide, chirality-independent band gaps (∼4.74 eV), yet their transmission functions differ markedly, leading to pronounced chirality-dependent variations in electrical conductance and power factor. The (19,0) scroll consistently exhibits the highest power factor, whereas the (15,0) scroll exhibits the lowest. The Seebeck coefficient exhibits weak chirality dependence overall, decreasing slightly with temperature, except for (17,0) and (18,0), which display anomalous increases at 600–700 K. The electron thermal conductance increases sharply (by a factor of 8.5–13.5) from 200 to 700 K with minimal chirality sensitivity. Crucially, the electronic thermoelectric figure of merit 𝑍 𝑇 𝑒 is governed primarily by the Seebeck coefficient and declines with temperature for all chiralities. The highest 𝑍 𝑇 𝑒 values are achieved for the (15,0) scroll (4.22 at 200 K and 3.40 at 300 K), whereas the (19,0) scroll exhibits remarkably stable 𝑍 𝑇 𝑒 (∼2.5–2.9) above 300 K. These results establish chirality engineering as an effective strategy for tailoring both the magnitude and thermal stability of thermoelectric performance in h-BNNSs.
articles.summary_en: A modeling study finds that h-BN nanoscroll chirality strongly affects electrical conductance, power factor, and electronic thermoelectric efficiency under ballistic transport. The results identify specific chiralities with higher performance and thermal stability, supporting chirality engineering for nanoscale thermoelectric devices.

articles.title_original: Amorphous Dielectric‐Integrated Retina‐Inspired HfS 2 Devices with Enhanced Synaptic Plasticity for Neuromorphic Vision Assistance
articles.title_en: Oxygen-Engineered HfS₂ Devices Improve Neuromorphic Vision Performance
articles.excerpt_original: ABSTRACT Realizing neuromorphic functionalities in field‐effect transistors (FETs) requires precise modulation of multilevel conductance states with robust retention. Two‐dimensional (2D) semiconductor FETs, however, often suffer from a limited synaptic weight dynamic range and short retention times because of inadequate charge dynamics in the channel. This results from the low‐k dielectric nature of the channel, which provides limited and unstable carrier storage sites and insufficient capacitive coupling. This study expands the weight dynamic range by forming a weight‐control dielectric through oxygen plasma treatment of HfS 2 , producing an HfO x /HfS 2 heterostructure. This engineered interface strengthens gate coupling and enables charge trapping via tailored defect states that act as dynamic storage centers, thereby providing tunable conductance and improved retention. Electrical characterization of the HfO x /HfS 2 FETs reveals a tenfold increase in the ON/OFF ratio and enhanced hysteresis. Under optical illumination, the devices exhibit high photoconductive gain and stable synaptic behavior, including a 67.38% larger dynamic range for long‐term potentiation/depression driven by trap‐mediated charge dynamics. This synaptic plasticity is leveraged to demonstrate optical encoding/decoding, in‐memory OR logic, and pattern‐recognition functionality, highlighting the potential of oxygen‐plasma‐engineered HfS 2 FETs for neuromorphic processors and integrated logic‐in‐memory systems.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed HfOₓ/HfS₂ field-effect transistors using oxygen plasma treatment to enhance charge trapping, conductance control, retention, and photoconductive gain. The devices demonstrated improved synaptic plasticity, optical encoding and decoding, in-memory logic, and pattern recognition for neuromorphic processors.

articles.title_original: Colossal visible birefringence and ultraviolet hyperbolicity in wide bandgap semiconductor CuAlO2
articles.title_en: CuAlO2 Shows Strong Visible Birefringence and UV Hyperbolicity
articles.excerpt_original: Materials combining colossal birefringence with a wide bandgap are of considerable interest for miniaturized photonics, yet remain rare because strong optical transitions that enhance birefringence usually introduce optical loss. Here we show that CuAlO2 exhibits colossal ultraviolet–visible birefringence alongside a wide bandgap. Spectroscopic ellipsometry on millimeter-sized single crystals reveals a sharp, intense lowest-energy transition near 3.78 eV exclusively in the ab-plane, yielding a maximum birefringence ∣Δn∣max = 3.67, and ∣Δn∣ > 0.5 throughout the visible range, with a direct band gap of 3.71 eV. The same transition generates a Type-II hyperbolic window between two ultraviolet epsilon-near-zero points. First-principles calculations and optical selection rules attribute this anisotropy to Cu-dominated band-edge states and a dipole-allowed Cu dz2-to-px/y transition enabled by the linear O–Cu–O dumbbell structure. These results establish CuAlO2 as a natural oxide platform that bridges broadband low-loss birefringence and ultraviolet hyperbolic photonics. Materials combining large optical anisotropy with a wide band gap are desirable for broadband anisotropic photonics. Here, the authors show for CuAlO2 a colossal ultraviolet–visible optical anisotropy with a maximum birefringence of 3.67 alongside a wide direct band gap of 3.71 eV.
articles.summary_en: Academic research reports that wide-bandgap semiconductor CuAlO2 combines a direct band gap of 3.71 eV with maximum birefringence of 3.67 and a Type-II ultraviolet hyperbolic window. The findings position CuAlO2 as a potential platform for miniaturized anisotropic and ultraviolet photonics.

articles.title_original: Direct growth of crystalline spinel GaON films: A wide-bandgap mixed-anion semiconductor
articles.title_en: Direct Growth of Crystalline GaON Films Enables Wide-Bandgap Semiconductor Research
articles.excerpt_original: Mixed-anion semiconductors offer opportunities for bandgap engineering beyond conventional multication alloys, but competing phases and disorder complicate their synthesis and the identification of their electronic properties. Gallium oxynitride (GaON) could connect the technologically important GaN and Ga2O3 systems, yet establishing a clear relation between its crystal structure, composition and bandgap remains challenging. Here we report the direct growth of crystalline spinel gamma-GaON films by nitrogen-plasma-assisted pulsed-laser deposition. Varying the nitrogen and oxygen supply yields monoclinic beta-Ga2O3, predominantly disordered films and crystalline spinel GaON. Complementary diffraction, atomic-resolution microscopy and elemental analysis establish the spinel structure and nitrogen incorporation. Temperature-dependent photocurrent spectroscopy reveals a clear redshift of the crystalline gamma-GaON response, supporting assignment of a band-edge transition near 4.3 eV at room temperature. These results open opportunities to investigate mixed-anion wide-bandgap semiconductor physics and develop heterostructures.
articles.summary_en: Researchers report direct growth of crystalline spinel gallium oxynitride (GaON) films using nitrogen-plasma-assisted pulsed-laser deposition. The films show a band-edge transition near 4.3 eV, supporting future mixed-anion semiconductor heterostructure development.

articles.title_original: Low-noise Pauli-consistent ensemble Monte Carlo for graphene with electron-electron scattering
articles.title_en: Low-Noise Monte Carlo Modeling of Electron Scattering in Graphene
articles.excerpt_original: We investigate Pauli-consistent ensemble Monte Carlo simulations of graphene with explicit intraband electron-electron scattering. To reduce the cost of electron-electron proposal-rate evaluation, we introduce a sampled-partner approximation that replaces the full partner-cell sum by uniform sampling from the instantaneous ensemble, while leaving the event-level collision step unchanged. Comparison with the full-sum reference shows close agreement together with a substantial reduction in computational cost, enabling large-ensemble low-noise simulations. In this regime, systematic oscillatory components become clearly resolved in ensemble-averaged time traces. We show that these oscillations are numerical and originate from deterministic drift on the discretized momentum-space grid. We also discuss a procedure for reducing their impact in recorded observables without modifying the underlying Monte Carlo dynamics.
articles.summary_en: Researchers introduce a sampled-partner approximation for Pauli-consistent ensemble Monte Carlo simulations of graphene with electron–electron scattering. The method substantially reduces computational cost while preserving agreement with full-sum simulations and helps identify numerical oscillations caused by discretized momentum-space drift.

articles.title_original: Mixed –N/–O Surface Terminations Enable Fast Ammonium-Ion Storage in Ti3C2T x MXene
articles.title_en: Mixed Surface Terminations Accelerate Ammonium-Ion Storage in MXene
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Aqueous ammonium-ion batteries are promising for safety, low cost, and fast energy storage. However, the influence of electrode surface chemistry on NH4+ storage remains poorly understood. Two-dimensional Ti3C2Tx MXene, with metallic conductivity, tunable interlayer spacing, and abundant surface terminations, serves as an ideal platform to elucidate NH4+ storage mechanisms. Herein, the role of MXene surface termination in regulating NH4+ storage behavior is systematically investigated using density functional theory calculations and experimental validation. The calculations reveal that the –N terminations offer moderate NH4+ adsorption and high electronic conductivity for rapid charge transfer and ion transport, whereas the –O terminations exhibit stronger ion affinity and enhanced surface stability. Importantly, the mixed –N/–O terminations effectively balance adsorption strength and transition-state stabilization, resulting in the lowest NH4+ migration barrier among the modeled pathways. The calculations employ idealized vacuum-separated surfaces with isolated NH4+ and do not explicitly include solvation or electrolyte effects. Guided by these findings, a mixed –N/–O terminated Ti3C2Tx MXene is constructed via a urea-assisted hydrothermal strategy. The optimized NTC-20 electrode delivers 107 mAh g–1 at 1 A g–1, retains 67% capacity at 10 A g–1, and maintains 91% capacity after 10,000 cycles. Ex situ XRD, XPS, and FTIR analyses are consistent with reversible NH4+-associated changes in the local chemical environment and possible storage involving Ti–N···H–N and Ti–O···H–N interactions. Furthermore, the NTC-20//MnO2/CNTs full cell achieves an energy density of 26.7 Wh kg–1 at 1.3 kW kg–1. The results support a dominant role for mixed –N/–O terminations in regula
articles.summary_en: ACS researchers show that mixed nitrogen and oxygen terminations on Ti3C2Tx MXene reduce ammonium-ion migration barriers and improve charge-transfer behavior. The optimized electrode delivered 107 mAh g−1, retained 67% capacity at 10 A g−1, and maintained 91% capacity after 10,000 cycles, although modeling did not include solvation or electrolyte effects.

articles.title_original: ENHANCED DRY SLIDING TRIBOLOGICAL AND MECHANICAL PERFORMANCE OF EPOXY HYBRID NANOCOMPOSITES REINFORCED WITH MWCNTs AND NIOBIUM MXENE
articles.title_en: MWCNT–Niobium MXene Epoxy Nanocomposites Improve Strength and Wear Resistance
articles.excerpt_original: The development of multifunctional polymer nanocomposites with enhanced mechanical, tribological and electrical performance is a significant challenge for advanced engineering applications. The epoxy-based hybrid nanocomposites reinforced with functionalized multi-walled carbon nanotubes (FMWCNTs) and niobium-based MXene (Nb2CTx) were systematically investigated to establish strong structure–property relationships in this study. A series of composites (ECnNx1–ECnNx5) was prepared by incorporating the hybrid fillers in different weight fractions and their performances were evaluated in terms of tensile, microhardness, dry sliding wear and electrical conductivity analysis. The results indicate that the one-dimensional MWCNTs and two-dimensional Nb2CTx nanosheets have a strong synergistic interaction, which significantly enhances the performance. Among these compositions, ECnNx3 exhibited the optimum properties with a maximum tensile strength of 68.54 MPa, which is about 90% higher than that of neat epoxy. Tribological analysis showed a considerable reduction in wear rate as much as 84 % at lower loads and stable performance was observed under increased loading conditions. The maximum value of microhardness was 56 HV, which shows an increased resistance to local deformation. Electrical conductivity results confirmed the formation of an effective percolation network facilitating the enhanced electron transport. Morphological analysis of the worn and fractured surfaces indicated a brittle to ductile transition and identified mechanisms such as crack deflection, fiber bridging and tribofilm formation as contributing factors to improved performance. However, the addition of too much filler resulted in agglomeration and reduced efficiency.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed epoxy hybrid nanocomposites reinforced with functionalized multi-walled carbon nanotubes and niobium MXene nanosheets. An optimized formulation increased tensile strength by about 90% and reduced dry-sliding wear by up to 84%, while excessive filler caused agglomeration and lower performance.

articles.title_original: Sub-10 nm High-Performance P-Type Transistors Based on Two-Dimensional HfX2 (X = Cl, Br, I): A Density Functional Theory–Nonequilibrium Green’s Function Study
articles.title_en: DFT Study Identifies HfX₂ as Promising Sub-10 nm p-Type FET Channels
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract As conventional Moore’s Law approaches physical scaling limits, the semiconductor industry has entered the post-Moore era, and two-dimensional (2D) semiconductors have emerged as candidate channel materials. Meanwhile, the lack of high-performance (HP) p-type field-effect transistors (FETs) hinders the development of high-efficiency complementary circuits. In this work, we systematically investigate the electronic structures and ballistic transport properties of monolayer HfX2 (X = Cl, Br, I) using first-principles calculations in combination with the nonequilibrium Green’s function (NEGF) method. The results show that 2D HfCl2, HfBr2, and HfI2 are indirect-band-gap semiconductors with band gaps of 0.85–1.03 eV and exhibit isotropy in the hole effective mass: m0 denotes the rest of a free electron. The hole effective mass is 0.30–0.38 m0 along the x and y direction. When the channel length is 5 nm, HfCl2, HfBr2, and HfI2 MOSFETs yield ballistic-performance upper-limit on-state currents Ion of 1197, 1087, and 1111 μA/μm, respectively. Moreover, HfI2 FETs with channel lengths ranging from 5 to 9 nm all meet the high-performance device requirements defined by the International Technology Roadmap for Semiconductors (ITRS). The comprehensive material performance demonstrates that monolayer HfX2 are promising p-type channel materials for next-generation high-speed and low-power 2D FETs.
articles.summary_en: A density functional theory and nonequilibrium Green’s function study evaluates monolayer HfCl₂, HfBr₂, and HfI₂ for p-type MOSFETs. Simulations predict ballistic on-state currents above 1,000 μA/μm at 5 nm, with HfI₂ meeting specified high-performance requirements from 5–9 nm channel lengths.

articles.title_original: Stacking-tuned interfacial electrostatics and nonadiabatic carrier dynamics in ZnAl2Te4/CdAl2Te4 van der Waals photovoltaic heterostructures
articles.title_en: Stacking tunes carrier dynamics in ZnAl₂Te₄/CdAl₂Te₄ photovoltaic heterostructures
articles.summary_en: Researchers investigated how layer stacking affects interfacial electrostatics and nonadiabatic carrier dynamics in ZnAl₂Te₄/CdAl₂Te₄ van der Waals heterostructures. The findings could inform the design of next-generation semiconductor photovoltaic devices.

articles.title_original: Graphene Materials With Anomalous Infrared Emissivity Yet Superb Chemical Stability
articles.title_en: Chemically Stable Graphene Achieves Record-Low Infrared Emissivity
articles.excerpt_original: ABSTRACT Low infrared emissivity materials (i.e., metallic materials) are of significance for thermal radiation regulation. However, the easy‐corrosion susceptibility and poor chemical stability are common bottleneck issues that affect their applications. We report a versatile electronic structure modulation strategy for low infrared (IR) emissivity graphene by engineering the surface chemistry of precursor graphene oxide and the followed reduction/doping process. The fabrication protocols minimize the irreparable disruption of the intrinsic graphitic structure and enable controllable assembly of nanosheets by suppressing formation of carboxyl groups. More significantly, the convenient reduction and halogen doping effects synergistically minimize electron scattering and enhance interfacial charge transport. The low‐defective graphitic structure and the ordered multiscale architecture, as well as halogen doping effect, afford exceptional carrier mobility (∼27.1 cm 2 V −1 s −1 ), carrier density (5.73 × 10 20 cm −3 ), and electrical conductivity comparable to highly oriented pyrolytic graphite. Surprisingly, the anomalous metallic response gives the lowest IR emissivity (0.15, 8–14 µm) for carbon materials, comparable to MXene and traditional metallic materials. The large‐scale processability and outstanding long‐term stability under chemical conditions offer new insights for the potential infrared applications of graphene materials.
articles.summary_en: Researchers engineered reduced and halogen-doped graphene materials with metallic-like conductivity and infrared emissivity as low as 0.15 across 8–14 µm. The scalable processing and chemical stability indicate potential for infrared thermal-radiation regulation applications.

articles.title_original: Multicomponent Magnetic Domain Walls in Rhombohedral Graphene
articles.title_en: Study reveals multicomponent magnetic domain walls in rhombohedral graphene
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Spatial textures of magnetic order, such as domain walls and skyrmions, are fundamental objects in magnetism. In rhombohedral multilayer graphene, magnetic order involves spin and valley degrees of freedom, opening the possibility of qualitatively new spatial textures. Here, we explore this possibility through a microscopic study of a one-dimensional domain wall in the valley-imbalanced quarter-metal phase of rhombohedral graphene. We uncover two different classes of domain walls. One resembles a conventional magnetic domain wall, locally rotating between the two bulk states, whereas the other is intrinsically multicomponent and explores states that are not occupied in either bulk domain. Which texture is realized is controlled by the competition between intervalley Hund's coupling and spin-orbit coupling, and we identify experimental signatures to distinguish them. For a superconducting junction formed across the wall, we further show that the superconducting phase difference couples directly to the intervalley-coherent phase of the texture, allowing precession of this internal phase to generate a voltage. This mechanism provides an explanation for the resistive domain walls recently observed in chiral superconductors [arXiv2605.13303] and predicts accompanying magnetization oscillations that could be detected using GHz-frequency AC probes. Our theory establish a microscopic connection between multicomponent magnetic textures, their internal dynamics, and superconducting transport.
articles.summary_en: Researchers model two distinct magnetic domain-wall classes in rhombohedral multilayer graphene, governed by intervalley Hund’s coupling and spin–orbit coupling. The work links these textures to superconducting transport and predicts magnetization oscillations detectable with GHz-frequency probes.

articles.title_original: Bio-inspired Dual-Mode Cooling Hydrogel Composite for Passive Heat Dissipation of Photovoltaic Panels
articles.title_en: Bio-inspired Hydrogel Composite Enables Passive PV Cooling
articles.excerpt_original: Photovoltaic (PV) panels experience pronounced efficiency loss and reliability degradation at elevated operating temperatures, creating an urgent demand for efficient thermal management. Conventional active cooling approaches, however, are constrained by high energy consumption and system complexity, restricting their applicability. Inspired by the thermoregulation strategy of the land snail Theba pisana, this work reports a dual-mode cooling hydrogel composite that integrates evaporative and radiative cooling in one material system, enabling passive thermal management of PV panels. The hydrogel composite, composed of sodium polyacrylate (PAAS), anhydrous calcium chloride (CaCl2), and hexagonal boron nitride (h-BN), enables sustained moisture sorption and release, while maintaining high solar reflectance and broadband mid-infrared emissivity. When integrated with the backside of a PV panel, the composite enables coupled evaporative-radiative heat dissipation, while its high solar reflectance can further reduce backside solar heat gain. Under direct sunlight, the composite achieves a temperature reduction of 17.8 °C on a simulated heat-generating device. When applied to a commercial PV panel, it lowers the operating temperature by up to 17.9 °C and increases the maximum output power by 7.1%. The hydrogel composite also exhibits intrinsic self-adhesion, flame retardancy, and stability during prolonged outdoor exposure, underscoring its potential for reliable and scalable PV thermal management. This work demonstrates a multifunctional biomimetic materials strategy for passive thermal management.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a sodium polyacrylate–calcium chloride–hexagonal boron nitride hydrogel combining evaporative and radiative cooling for photovoltaic panels. It reduced panel temperature by up to 17.9 °C and increased maximum output power by 7.1% under reported test conditions.

articles.title_original: Rough-Surface-Dominated Knudsen Gas Flow in Heterogeneous Nanochannels
articles.title_en: Rough Surfaces Suppress Gas Flow in Graphene Nanochannels
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Gas flow in heterogeneous nanochannels with asymmetric wall properties is important for many advanced technologies, yet how dissimilar surfaces synergistically govern the Knudsen gas flow remains elusive. Here, we combine molecular dynamics simulations with grand canonical Monte Carlo methods to systematically investigate gas flow in heterogeneous nanochannels composed of smooth walls (graphene and h-BN) and rough walls (MoS2 and SiO2) with channel heights ranging from the angstrom scale to the nanoscale. The results show that gas flux in heterogeneous nanochannels is consistently lower than the arithmetic mean of the fluxes in the corresponding homogeneous channels and that this deviation is amplified under angstrom-scale extreme confinement. This rough-surface-dominated behavior arises from the nonlinear relationship between the tangential momentum accommodation coefficient and gas flux. Because gas molecules collide with the two walls with nearly equal probability in the Knudsen regime, the tangential momentum accommodation coefficient of heterogeneous channels under weak to moderate confinement is close to the average of the corresponding homogeneous values. This averaged tangential momentum accommodation coefficient, however, yields a flux biased toward the rough channel value rather than the average. In addition, under angstrom-scale confinement, asymmetric wall potentials further amplify the internal energy corrugation, enhancing momentum dissipation, and suppressing flux. These findings reveal the mechanisms of Knudsen gas flow in heterogeneous nanochannels and provide guidance for predictive modeling and rational design of asymmetric nanofluidic devices.
articles.summary_en: Molecular simulations show that heterogeneous nanochannels combining graphene or h-BN smooth walls with rough MoS₂ or SiO₂ walls have lower Knudsen gas flux than predicted by averaging homogeneous channels. The findings clarify confinement-dependent momentum dissipation and could guide asymmetric nanofluidic device design.

articles.title_original: Pseudo-relativistic fermions and topological states in zinc-blende semiconductors and their heterostructures (Habilitation thesis)
articles.title_en: Habilitation thesis examines topological states in semiconductor heterostructures
articles.excerpt_original: Tracing my scientific path from many-body physics in semiconductor nanostructures to topological quantum matter, this Habilitation à diriger des recherches (HDR) memoir presents only part of my research since defending two PhD theses in Toulouse and Nizhny Novgorod in 2011. Focusing on pseudo-relativistic fermions and topological states in zinc-blende semiconductors and their heterostructures, it highlights my independent research program: identifying physical problems, developing predictive theories, and initiating new directions with experimentalists. The first part addresses Kane fermions in bulk HgCdTe: temperature-driven band inversion, domain-wall states, the collapse of Landau levels in crossed electric and magnetic fields, and disorder-induced topological transitions. The second examines pressure-, temperature-, and disorder-driven phase transitions in single and double HgTe quantum wells (QWs), including bilayer-graphene-like semimetals and a two-dimensional higher-order topological insulator (2D HOTI) phase beyond the minimal BHZ model. The third develops three-layer InAs/Ga(In)Sb QWs as a III-V platform for massless Dirac fermions, large-gap quantum spin Hall insulators, 2D HOTI phases, and semimetals with quadratic band touching, and discusses InAs$_{x}$Sb$_{1-x}$/InAs$_{y}$Sb$_{1-y}$ heterostructures as a promising alternative. Several of these predictions are supported by experimental observations, including quantized helical edge transport up to 60 K and the unconventional quantum Hall effect. Defended on March 25, 2026, at the University of Montpellier. Jury: Michel GOIRAN (chair and rapporteur, LNCMI-CNRS, Toulouse); Alexey KAVOKIN (rapporteur, Westlake University, Hangzhou); Robson FERREIRA (rapporteur, LPENS-CNRS, Paris); Alexei BARANOV (member, IES-C
articles.summary_en: A University of Montpellier habilitation thesis develops theoretical and experimental insights into pseudo-relativistic fermions, quantum spin Hall phases, and higher-order topological states in HgTe, HgCdTe, InAs/GaSb, and related semiconductor heterostructures. The work includes graphene-like semimetal behavior but does not study graphene itself.

articles.title_original: Analysis of the Relationship Between the Proportion of Surface Atoms and Light Emission Competition in Semiconductor Nanomaterials
articles.title_en: Surface Atom Ratio Governs Light-Emission Competition in Semiconductor Nanomaterials
articles.excerpt_original: Because of their quantum size effects and surface effects, semiconductor nanomaterials show a wide range of optical properties, making them a core part of strategic industries like high-definition displays, solid-state lighting, and biomedical detection. Its light-emitting mechanism mainly includes exciton emission and defect emission. The coexistence and competition between the two is one of the key factors affecting performance. But traditional studies mostly attribute it separately to quantum size effects and surface effects, lacking a unified structural parameter. This article introduces 'surface atom ratio' as a parameter to uniformly describe this competitive relationship, and also analyzes its role as a bridge connecting quantum size effects and surface effects. Using a theoretical analysis approach, starting from the three major effects of nanomaterials, the aim is to derive the relationship between the proportion of surface atoms and size, and explain their connection to enhanced quantum confinement and defect state density; through systematically analyzing the effects of size and surface passivation on competition, the rules of luminescence competition centered on the proportion of surface atoms are summarized. This article found that this parameter can indeed effectively regulate the coexistence and competition between the two, and provides a reference for designing nanomaterials with high luminescence efficiency in a measurable way.
articles.summary_en: A theoretical study proposes surface atom ratio as a unified parameter linking quantum confinement and defect-state effects in semiconductor nanomaterials. The framework may guide the design of higher-efficiency luminescent materials for displays, solid-state lighting, and biomedical detection.

articles.title_original: Irreducible sub-nm2 ferroelectric domains by 2D-flat polar band in perovskite superlattices
articles.title_en: Perovskite Superlattices Enable Sub-nm² Ferroelectric Domains
articles.excerpt_original: Flat polar phonon bands in ferroelectrics have been envisioned to realize irreducibly small domains for achieving the highest memory density. However, such bands are quite uncommon, with only a one-dimensional flat polar band discovered in ferroelectric hafnia, which gives rise to irreducibly narrow, line-type domains with a half-unit-cell width of 2.7 Å. Here, we report the discovery of a two-dimensional flat polar band in the ferroelectric (BaTiO 3 ) 1 /(BaXO 3 ) 1 superlattice (X = Zr, Sn), which generates extremely localized, noninteracting dipoles within its quarter-unit-cell area that form quasi-degenerate states of irreducible sub-nm² ferroelectric domains. The estimated ferroelectric domain density, exceeding 300 \({{\mathrm{Tbit}}}/{{\mathrm{cm}}}^2\) (assuming one bit per domain) represents a record high among the known ferroelectrics, with independently switchable dipoles at low voltages. The ferroelectric phase hosting two-dimensional flat bands constitutes a competing ground state across superlattice stacking directions and thus can be experimentally realized in both freestanding structures and epitaxial growth on MgO substrates. This discovery opens unprecedented opportunities to explore multidimensional flat polar bands in ferroelectrics and to engineer ultra-dense and low-power memory devices.
articles.summary_en: Researchers report a two-dimensional flat polar band in BaTiO₃/BaXO₃ (X=Zr, Sn) superlattices, producing independently switchable ferroelectric domains smaller than 1 nm². The structures could support ultra-dense, low-power memory exceeding 300 Tbit/cm², with potential realization in freestanding films and MgO-supported epitaxial growth.

articles.title_original: Preliminary mechanical and environmental assessment of bituminous mixtures including a graphene-based compound
articles.title_en: Graphene–Recycled Plastic Additive Improves Asphalt Performance
articles.excerpt_original: The constant increase in the performance request and the need to preserve the environment for future generations drive to the development of sustainable technologies and materials. Within this framework, extending pavement service life, reducing maintenance frequency, and limiting the consumption of virgin raw materials are key targets. Also, the reuse of reclaimed and end-of-life materials can contribute to these objectives, provided that the resulting mixtures maintain adequate mechanical and functional performance. In this perspective, this study investigates an innovative graphene-based additive incorporating selected recycled hard plastics for asphalt wearing courses. For this purpose, different mixtures have been produced with the additive via dry process and subjected to both functional and mechanical characterization, in order to compare the modified solutions with conventional and high-performance reference mixtures. The test results indicate that the use of a compound based on graphene and recycled hard plastics can improve selected mechanical performance indicators of the mixtures, especially indirect tensile strength, stiffness and rutting resistance. The investigated surface indicators remained within the relevant specification limits, although some variations with respect to the reference mixtures were observed. For a more robust evaluation of the experimental mixtures, they were also comparatively studied in terms of environmental impact using the Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) methodology. Within the adopted cradle-to-gate boundary, the results indicate reductions in energy consumption and related emissions for the modified mixtures. Overall, the findings support the technical feasibility of the proposed additive for the investigated asphalt mixtures, while
articles.summary_en: A study finds that a graphene-based compound incorporating recycled hard plastics can improve asphalt mixtures’ indirect tensile strength, stiffness and rutting resistance. Life-cycle assessment also indicates lower energy use and emissions within the cradle-to-gate boundary, supporting preliminary technical feasibility for pavement applications.

articles.title_original: Electron-Mediated Phonon Polaritons in Quantum Cavities
articles.title_en: Electron-mediated phonon polaritons in quantum cavities
articles.excerpt_original: Phonon-photon coupling in quantum materials is commonly treated as an effective direct interaction, neglecting the crucial role played by electrons. Here we develop a gauge-invariant theory of cavity phonon polaritons that captures electronic screening, dissipation, and hybridization. We show that screening can suppress polariton formation in metals, severely constraining cavity control of phonon-mediated superconductivity. By contrast, interband electronic resonances in time-reversal-symmetric gapped systems can strongly enhance phonon-photon coupling, enabling robust polariton formation down to the monolayer limit despite electronic absorption. We illustrate these effects in NbSe2, hBN, and gapped graphene. Finally, we show that gauge invariance enforces photon decoupling from a critical soft phonon, establishing a general no-go mechanism for photon condensation.
articles.summary_en: Researchers develop a gauge-invariant theory showing that electronic screening, dissipation and hybridization critically shape cavity phonon polaritons. The work identifies conditions enabling robust polariton formation in gapped graphene down to the monolayer limit, with implications for quantum photonics and phonon-mediated superconductivity.

articles.title_original: Exciton condensation from level repulsion: Application to bilayer graphene
articles.title_en: Exciton Condensation in Bilayer Graphene Driven by Level Repulsion
articles.summary_en: Academic research examines how level repulsion can produce exciton condensation in bilayer graphene. The work advances understanding of collective quantum states relevant to graphene-based semiconductor devices, without reporting a commercial application.

articles.title_original: Superconductivity and charge density waves in graphene-based materials
articles.title_en: Review Examines Superconductivity and Charge-Density Waves in Graphene
articles.excerpt_original: Graphene-based materials have emerged as a versatile platform for exploring strongly correlated quantum phenomena, particularly superconductivity (SC) and charge density waves (CDWs), owing to their highly tunable electronic structure, reduced dimensionality, and sensitivity to external perturbations. While pristine monolayer graphene is not intrinsically superconducting and exhibits limited propensity toward charge ordering, a variety of engineered graphene systems have demonstrated remarkable SC and CDW phases through mechanisms involving doping, intercalation, proximity coupling, strain, and moiré superlattice engineering. The discovery of correlated insulating states and superconductivity in magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene has revolutionized the field by revealing unprecedented opportunities for studying unconventional pairing mechanisms and competing electronic orders in a purely carbon-based material platform. This review critically examines the current understanding of emergent SC and CDW in graphene-derived systems. We survey the diverse classes of graphene-based superconductors, including chemically doped and intercalated graphene, twisted bi- and trilayer graphene structures, and proximity-induced superconducting heterostructures, emphasizing the role of electron-phonon coupling, flat-band formation, and interfacial effects. Subsequently, we discuss the fundamental origins of CDW formation in graphene, focusing on electron-phonon interactions, Peierls instability, Fermi-surface nesting, defect engineering, doping, heterostructure design, and moiré-induced electronic reconstruction. The coexistence and competition between SC and charge-ordered phases, as revealed by scanning tunneling microscopy (STM), angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES), tra
articles.summary_en: The review surveys superconducting and charge-density-wave phases in engineered graphene systems, including doped, intercalated, twisted-layer, strained, and proximity-coupled structures. It highlights moiré engineering and flat-band formation as key routes to correlated quantum states and unconventional pairing.

articles.title_original: Multipeak dual-polarization nonreciprocity with wavelength-selective directionality in a Ge–Si/graphene/InAs metasurface
articles.title_en: Ge–Si/Graphene/InAs Metasurface Enables Wavelength-Selective Nonreciprocity
articles.summary_en: Researchers report a metasurface combining Ge–Si, graphene and InAs that provides multipeak dual-polarization nonreciprocity with wavelength-selective directional control. The work indicates potential relevance to tunable photonic and optoelectronic components, although application readiness is not established.

articles.title_original: Spacer-mediated gold nanocube arrays for edge-localized excitonic enhancement in monolayer MoS2
articles.title_en: Gold nanocube arrays enhance excitonic emission in monolayer MoS2
articles.excerpt_original: Plasmonic nanostructures offer an effective route for enhancing light-matter interaction in atomically thin semiconductors, whose optical response is intrinsically limited by their subnanometer active thickness. Here, we numerically investigate excitonic enhancement in monolayer (ML) Molybdenum Disulfide (MoS2) coupled to size-tuned gold (Au) nanocube arrays separated by thin aluminum oxide (Al2O3) and hexagonal boron nitride (h-BN) spacer layers. By varying the nanocube side length, the localized surface plasmon resonance is tuned across the visible spectral range to modulate the A- and B-excitonic transitions of monolayer MoS2.We show that the nanocube-size-dependent spectral redshift can be further controlled through the spacer material and thickness, enabling systematic tuning of the near-field distribution, carrier generation rate, antenna quantum yield, and radiative decay enhancement. Localized plasmonic confinement yields excitation-rate enhancements of up to 4.35 at B-excitonic transition (605 nm) and 3.66 at A-excitonic transition (650 nm), while the radiative decay-rate enhancement exceeds 80, leading to 350-fold local photoluminescence enhancement. Although both A- and B-excitonic channels are enhanced simultaneously, their relative contributions depend on nanocube size, spacer material, and spacer thickness, indicating wavelength-dependent excitonic modulation rather than strict exciton-selective switching. These findings establish Au nanocube arrays as a simple, scalable, and tunable plasmonic platform for enhancing excitonic carrier generation and emission in ML MoS2.
articles.summary_en: Numerical modeling shows that gold nanocube arrays separated from monolayer MoS2 by Al2O3 or h-BN spacers can tune plasmonic resonances and enhance excitonic light emission. The modeled platform produced up to 350-fold local photoluminescence enhancement, supporting tunable optical and semiconductor-device research.

articles.title_original: Light‐Driven Phase Engineering in 2D Materials From Mechanistic Assignment to Ambient Near‐Field Control
articles.title_en: Light-Driven Phase Engineering Enables Ambient Nanoscale Control of 2D Materials
articles.excerpt_original: Light-driven phase transitions and transformations provide a route for post-synthesis control of structure, charge order, ferroic polarization, chemistry, and local transport in 2D materials. Optical excitation can activate carrier dynamics, phonon coupling, heating, strain redistribution, vacancy formation, surface reactions, and substrate-mediated effects during one experiment. Mechanistic assignment consequently requires separate identification of the process initiating conversion and the mechanism preserving the modified material. We organize representative experiments into seven practical classes based on the dominant experimentally supported mechanism and outline experimental criteria for distinguishing competing contributions. A quantitative workflow combines independent material verification, controlled perturbations, temporal measurements, and material-specific descriptors of conversion and stabilization. Far-field laser processing remains valuable for patterning and device fabrication, although diffraction-limited illumination averages over nanoscale heterogeneity. Tip-enhanced femtosecond excitation in scattering-type scanning near-field optical microscopy provides a complementary route by localizing excitation and linking nanoscale writing with local optical, structural, and chemical verification. Localized excitation can support reproducible ambient nanoscale phase control when excitation, phase identity, and retention are verified within one region.
articles.summary_en: Researchers classify mechanisms behind light-induced phase transitions in 2D materials and propose a workflow to distinguish conversion from stabilization. Tip-enhanced femtosecond excitation offers localized ambient phase control with nanoscale optical, structural, and chemical verification, supporting future device fabrication.

articles.title_original: Polariton-enhanced multi-dimensional mid-infrared response devices
articles.title_en: Review highlights polariton-enhanced graphene mid-infrared sensing devices
articles.excerpt_original: The mid-infrared (MIR, 2–25 μm) spectral range covers the molecular vibrational fingerprint region, two atmospheric windows (3–5 and 8–14 μm), and overlaps significantly with room-temperature blackbody radiation, making it invaluable for chemical and biomedical sensing, free-space communication, remote sensing, and thermal imaging. MIR response devices convert target characteristic information into detectable electrical, thermal, or optical signals, expanding the detection boundaries in critical application domains. However, conventional MIR response devices commonly face challenges such as cryogenic cooling dependence, large system volume, high cost, and reliance primarily on intensity response, making it difficult to identify complex backgrounds or camouflaged targets. MIR response devices designed based on polariton theory achieve on-chip acquisition of multi-dimensional optical field information including wavelength, intensity, and polarization through subwavelength-scale light field localization and mode control, promoting the evolution of MIR response devices from single intensity response to multi-dimensional information perception. This review discusses recent progress in polariton-enhanced multi-dimensional MIR response devices, detailing the working mechanisms of plasmon- and phonon-polaritons, and reviewing plasmon-enhanced devices based on metals, graphene, and black phosphorus, phonon-polariton-enhanced devices based on hexagonal boron nitride (hBN), α-MoO3, and silicon carbide (SiC), as well as the application status and inherent advantages of hybrid polaritons (graphene–metal, metal–SiO2, graphene–hBN/SiO2). This highlights that polariton enhancement plays a pivotal role in improving the sensitivity, integration, and information dimension acquisition of M
articles.summary_en: A review examines polariton-based mid-infrared devices that capture wavelength, intensity, and polarization information on chip. It covers graphene plasmonic devices and graphene–metal, graphene–hBN, and graphene–SiO₂ hybrid polaritons for sensing, communications, remote sensing, and thermal imaging.

articles.title_original: Carrier Dynamics in Low-Dimensional and Wide-Bandgap Materials Probed by Terahertz Magneto-Optical Spectroscopy
articles.title_en: THz Magneto-Optical Spectroscopy Maps Carrier Dynamics in Advanced Materials
articles.excerpt_original: Terahertz (THz) radiation lies between the microwave and infrared (0.1–10 THz, photon energies ~0.4–40 meV), an energy scale matching the low-energy excitations and picosecond (ps) relaxation of free carriers; this makes THz magneto-optical (MO) spectroscopy a powerful, contactless probe of carrier dynamics in electronic materials. In this review, we summarize the progress in using THz time-domain spectroscopy (TDS) in the Faraday geometry to study the MO properties of low-dimensional and wide-bandgap materials. We first introduce the experimental principles and the theoretical framework, centered on the generalized MO Drude–Smith model that accounts for photon-induced electronic backscattering, and outline how the longitudinal conductivity and the left- and right-handed circularly polarized MO conductivities or conductances are extracted. We also describe how key electronic parameters, the carrier density, relaxation time, effective mass, static dielectric constant, and localization factor, are determined, with the effective mass obtained under a non-cyclotron resonance condition. We then review and compare studies on representative systems, including monolayer and bilayer MoS2, nitrogen-doped carbon nanodots (N-CNDs), nitrogen-doped diamond, and neutron-irradiated hexagonal boron nitride (hBN). Across these systems, common magnetic-field trends emerge: the carrier density and localization factor decrease, while the relaxation time, effective mass, and dielectric constant increase. For nitrogen-doped diamond, the magnetic-field dependences of the Faraday rotation angle and ellipticity reveal a pronounced THz MO response, highlighting its potential as a THz polarization-rotation material. Finally, we discuss the current challenges and future prospects, including broader
articles.summary_en: A review examines terahertz magneto-optical spectroscopy as a contactless method for extracting carrier density, relaxation time, effective mass and localization in low-dimensional and wide-bandgap materials. Nitrogen-doped diamond shows strong Faraday rotation and ellipticity, indicating potential for THz polarization-rotation applications.
