articles.title_original: Energy levels of screened charged impurity in gapped graphene under magnetic field
articles.title_en: Study Models Charged-Impurity Energy Levels in Gapped Graphene
articles.excerpt_original: In this paper, we present a comprehensive theoretical study of the electronic states in gapped graphene in the presence of a charge impurity and a magnetic field. We focus on the impurity-induced modification of the Landau levels under the influence of an attractive or repulsive Coulomb potential. Since analytical solutions of the Dirac equation are not available in this case, the study is carried out using the Wentzel-Kramers-Brillouin (WKB) approach. Special attention is paid to the screening of the Coulomb potential in the presence of metallic gates situated at some distances from graphene sheet, as is commonly the case in experiments. Using both analytical and numerical methods, we determine the energy spectrum as a function of the magnetic field strength and impurity charge for screened and unscreened Coulomb potentials. Our results reveal a significant dependence of the energy levels for sample-to-gate distances of less than 50 nm.
articles.summary_en: Researchers theoretically analyze how screened and unscreened Coulomb impurities alter Landau levels in gapped graphene under magnetic fields. The study finds strong dependence on graphene-to-metallic-gate distance below 50 nm, offering insights for graphene electronic experiments and device modeling.

articles.title_original: Dual-Network Toughening of Aramid Nanofiber/MXene Core–Shell Fibers with Boosted Mechanical and Electrical Performance
articles.title_en: Aramid–MXene Core–Shell Fibers Improve Mechanical Stability for Strain Sensing
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract MXene-based fiber electronics have gained significant attention due to their superior performance. However, the potential applications are limited by drawbacks, including poor spinnability, inferior mechanical properties, and weak stability during practical applications. In this study, a core–shell fiber electronic was prepared via coaxial microfluidic spinning. Specifically, a dual-network architecture composed of an aramid nanofiber (ANF) entanglement network and an ANF-MXene hydrogen-bonding network was introduced in the core, while a protective encapsulation of ANFs was constructed in the shell. The MXene nanosheets were interconnected by the entangled ANFs and anchored via the ANF-MXene hydrogen-bonding network, leading to improved spinnability of the MXene suspension. Consequently, the resultant ANF/MXene fiber (AMF) exhibited enhanced mechanical properties. By incorporating thermochromic microcapsules into the shell layer, the AMF showed proof-of-concept thermochromic temperature indication and Joule-heating functions. Moreover, the enhanced stability of the ANF-MXene hybrid network holds significant potential in applications as stable strain sensors, enabling the precise detection of small deformations. This research presents a one-step fabrication method for high-performance fiber electronics with good mechanical properties, significantly broadening the application prospects of MXene-based electronics.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed coaxially spun aramid nanofiber/MXene core–shell fibers using dual-network reinforcement and protective encapsulation. The fibers combine improved mechanical stability with thermochromic indication, Joule heating, and potential low-deformation strain-sensing capabilities.

articles.title_original: Polyaniline-Modified MXene/Carbon Nanotube Scaffold Enabling High-Rate and Long-Cycle Zinc–Iodine Batteries
articles.title_en: Polyaniline-Modified MXene/CNT Scaffold Improves Zinc–Iodine Battery Performance
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Aqueous zinc–iodine (Zn–I2) batteries are attractive for large-scale energy storage because of their low cost and inherent safety. However, the practical use of an I2 cathode is severely restricted by poor electronic conductivity and the shuttle effect of soluble polyiodides. Herein, a synergistic scaffold composed of MXene and carbon nanotubes (CNTs) modified with protonated polyaniline (PANI) via electrostatic interactions was designed. The MXene/CNT scaffold ensures overall conductivity and structural integrity. The protonated PANI immobilizes iodine species through nitrogen-containing groups and accelerates their interconversion, effectively suppressing the shuttle effect. The MXene/CNTs/PANI-I2 cathode with an iodine loading of 43.96 wt % achieves a superior specific capacity of 150 mAh g–1 at a high rate of 20 C as well as excellent cycling stability over 10 000 cycles. This work offers a viable strategy for developing stable I2 cathodes for high-performance Zn–I2 batteries.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a protonated polyaniline-modified MXene/carbon nanotube scaffold for aqueous zinc–iodine batteries. The cathode achieved 150 mAh g⁻¹ at 20 C and remained stable for more than 10,000 cycles, indicating a promising research pathway for high-rate stationary energy storage.

articles.title_original: Enhanced Thermal Conductivity and Phase Stability of Pickering Emulsion Phase Change Materials via Hexagonal Boron Nitride and Their Applications in Device Thermal Management Conversion
articles.title_en: h-BN Composite Phase-Change Material Enhances Electronics Thermal Management
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract As electronic devices evolve toward higher integration and power density, localized heat accumulation poses greater challenges to device operational stability and safety. In this study, a water-in-oil (W/O) Pickering emulsion template method was employed to successfully prepare a hexagonal boron nitride h-BN-reinforced disodium hydrogen phosphate dodecahydrate/n-eicosane oil composite phase-change material (HPC-BN). This system employs Na2HPO4·12H2O as the aqueous phase and n-eicosane as the oil phase to form a water-in-oil Pickering emulsion, with h-BN introduced to establish thermal conduction pathways. The results indicate that the Pickering emulsion particles in the composite adhere tightly to the surface of the h-BN flakes, and the components exhibit good physical compatibility. This unique structure enables the composite to maintain a high latent heat of 193.8 J·g−1while increasing the thermal conductivity to 1.29 W·m−1·K−1, effectively slowing the temperature rise rate and limiting the maximum temperature of electronic devices in thermal management experiments. After 200 thermal cycles, the composite material still exhibits good thermal and structural stability, as well as satisfactory flame retardancy and corrosion resistance, providing insights for the application of composite phase-change energy storage materials in the field of passive thermal management for electronic devices.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a hexagonal boron nitride-reinforced phase-change composite with 193.8 J·g−1 latent heat and thermal conductivity of 1.29 W·m−1·K−1. The material limited temperature rise in electronic-device tests and retained thermal and structural stability after 200 cycles.

articles.title_original: Deterministic positioning accuracy of B centers in hBN by electron irradiation
articles.title_en: Electron Irradiation Enables Precise Positioning of hBN B Centers
articles.excerpt_original: Hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) is a promising material platform for quantum technologies, enabling both the realization of nanophotonic devices and the hosting of point defects that act as high-quality single-photon emitters (SPEs). Among these defects, B centers, which reproducibly emit at 436 nm, can be generated individually at predefined positions using electron beam irradiation, a crucial capability for top-down quantum photonics. Yet, the spatial accuracy of emitter creation strongly conditions the potential applications. Here, we generate arrays of individual B centers in a scanning electron microscope (SEM) with in-situ cathodoluminescence (CL) monitoring. We characterize the sources of random deviations from the target positions to identify the limitations to their deterministic positioning. In particular, we measure the distance between the electron beam and the emitter at the moment the emitter is created based on CL mapping. This approach provides a direct estimation of the spatial extent of the beam-emitter interaction. We find this contribution to be the main constraint to the emitter fabrication accuracy, yielding a standard deviation of 27 nm. Additional contributions, primarily from the finite density of UV-emitting carbon dimer precursors, increase the overall positional standard deviation to 40 nm. Our results highlight the possible improvements to the B center creation technique to reach sub-10 nm accuracy.
articles.summary_en: Researchers demonstrated deterministic creation of individual boron centers in hexagonal boron nitride using electron-beam irradiation with in-situ cathodoluminescence monitoring. Positioning accuracy was limited to a 40 nm standard deviation, with the study identifying pathways toward sub-10 nm accuracy for quantum photonics applications.

articles.title_original: The influence of fabrication adhesion temperature on the excitonic behavior of 2D MoS2/hBN heterostructures
articles.title_en: Adhesion temperature modulates excitonic emission in MoS₂/hBN heterostructures
articles.excerpt_original: Heterostructures are key components in photonic devices consisting of two-dimensional (2D) materials. Therefore, understanding the impact of their fabrication process parameters on their performances is of utmost importance. We fabricated MoS 2 /hBN heterostructures and investigated the effect of the adhesion temperature on their light emission. Raman analysis reveals that adhesion temperatures above ~ 100 ° C induce atomic modifications, manifested by redshifts of the E 2g and A 1g vibrational modes. Light-emission analysis revealed a lower emission intensity in the heterostructure than in bare MoS 2 , with a further reduction in intensity as the adhesion temperature increased. Additionally, photoluminescence (PL) analysis revealed that the A-excitons and trions dominate the light emission (jointly composing above 99% of the emission spectral weight), while the B-excitons contribution was negligible. Importantly, the adhesion temperature did not alter the charge-carrier concentration. Atomistic molecular dynamics simulation reveals that these changes result from thermal buckling induced by the thermal-expansion mismatch between the MoS 2 and hBN layers. Therefore, these insights identify the fabrication parameters that influence the light-emission characteristics of heterostructures and enable modulation of their excitonic emission, paving the way for the future development of optically engineered emitting devices.
articles.summary_en: Researchers found that adhesion temperatures above approximately 100°C cause atomic modifications and progressively reduce light emission in MoS₂/hBN heterostructures. Simulations attribute the changes to thermally induced buckling from thermal-expansion mismatch, providing guidance for optically engineered 2D photonic devices.

articles.title_original: Foreword
articles.title_en: Foreword: Boron’s Unique Chemistry
articles.excerpt_original: It is a truism that all of the chemical elements have a chemistry that is unique but an element's chemistry is, nevertheless, often similar to that of its nearest neighbours in the Periodic Table especially to those elements in the same vertical column we call a group.Indeed, the very origins of the Periodic Table reflect a recognition of chemical similarities between certain elements.Now many will argue that unique is not a gradable adjective and therefore its use should not be relativised with qualifiers such as 'more', 'almost' or 'very'.I will risk the ire of language purists, however, by stating that of all the elements, one can reasonably aver that the chemistry of boron is the most unique, but what basis could there be for such an assertion?There are certainly some compounds of boron that have similar properties to the corresponding compounds of its near neighbours but one need look no further than the boron hydrides (boranes), and their many derivatives, for evidence to support the claim that boron is somehow special.For the most part, the remarkable structures of these hydrides have no counterpart in the chemistry of any other element.A similar case can be made with regard to the structures of the allotropes of elemental boron and the multitude of borides than boron forms in combination with other elements.These examples by no means constitute an exhaustive list of boron's peculiarities but Boron: In Search of the Real Fifth Element By
articles.summary_en: This academic foreword introduces boron’s distinctive chemistry, emphasizing the unusual structures of boranes, boron allotropes, and borides. It provides general scientific context rather than reporting a specific research result or application.

articles.title_original: Ultrahigh Interfacial Thermal Conductance across GaN/BAs Interfaces via Atomic‐Level Engineering
articles.title_en: Atomic engineering boosts thermal conductance at GaN/BAs interfaces
articles.excerpt_original: ABSTRACT The integration of gallium nitride (GaN) with ultrahigh‐thermal‐conductivity boron arsenide (BAs) substrates represents a promising pathway for developing next‐generation high‐power devices. The heat dissipation capability of such integrated systems is fundamentally governed by thermal transport across GaN/BAs interfaces, and buffer layers such as Al 2 O 3 have been widely adopted to accommodate lattice mismatch and facilitate heterointegration. However, the atomic‐scale structural factors governing thermal transport across GaN/BAs interfaces remain unclear, limiting further improvements in interfacial thermal conductance. Herein, we propose an atomic‐scale interfacial structural‐uniformity strategy for engineering ultrahigh thermal conductance across GaN/BAs interfaces using molecular dynamics simulations augmented by machine‐learning interatomic potentials. We show that interfacial structural uniformity plays a more important role than individual bond strength in determining thermal transport across the investigated GaN/BAs interfaces. For instance, the As‐N‐terminated coherent interface exhibits the highest interfacial structural uniformity and achieves an ultrahigh interfacial thermal conductance of approximately 2000 MW·m − 2 ·K − 1 , representing a nearly eightfold enhancement over the experimentally reported Al 2 O 3 ‐mediated interface (250 MW·m −2 ·K −1 ). Finite‐element analysis indicates that this atomic‐scale optimization directly translates into device‐scale performance, leading to a substantial improvement in overall heat dissipation efficiency. These findings suggest that engineering interfacial structural uniformity offers a promising strategy for achieving high‐efficiency thermal management in next‐generation high‐power electronic devices.
articles.summary_en: Molecular-dynamics simulations using machine-learning interatomic potentials indicate that atomic-scale interfacial uniformity can raise GaN/BAs thermal conductance to approximately 2,000 MW·m⁻²·K⁻¹. Finite-element analysis suggests improved device-scale heat dissipation for high-power electronics compared with Al₂O₃-mediated interfaces.

articles.title_original: Principles and Techniques for Agentic Research in Experimental Physics
articles.title_en: Agentic AI Framework Demonstrated Across Experimental Physics Workflows
articles.excerpt_original: The use of artificial intelligence (AI) in physics research is increasingly common, yet few guidelines exist for its effective use. Starting with a principles-based approach, we outline a set of ten requirements for collaborative AI agents in experimental physics, spanning scientific norms, effective agent use, and domain expertise. We take a human-centered approach in which agents act as collaborators that amplify rather than replace the expertise of a human researcher (user) who directs the work and is responsible for its results. We then present a framework designed to enforce these requirements, detailing methods for improving off-the-shelf behavior of large language models (LLMs) with custom scaffolding and describing general-purpose scientific workflows and skills. In particular, we highlight the power of closed-loop campaigns where agents work iteratively toward a well-defined goal. We demonstrate the potential of this mode of research through six case studies in experimental physics, covering device design, hardware control, neural network optimization, physical model identification, and data analysis. All six case studies result in useful work products that add utility to our research, including a neural network architecture and solid-state quantum defect photodynamic model that substantially outperform our published work; a microwave waveguide design that extends a published design concept to a fabrication-ready device meeting our experimental constraints; a quantum control pulse sequence candidate that improves simulated performance by more than an order of magnitude; commissioning of an NMR spectrometer to $\sim$1~Hz frequency precision on live hardware; and finally a data-fitting pipeline that achieves, to our knowledge, the first reconstruction of the Isin
articles.summary_en: Researchers propose principles and a framework for using collaborative AI agents in experimental physics, emphasizing human oversight and closed-loop workflows. Six case studies report outputs including device designs, quantum-control optimization, hardware commissioning, and data-analysis tools.
verticals: Other — experimental physics and scientific AI

articles.title_original: Excitonic Physics in Emerging 2D Semiconductors: A First-Principles Many-Body Perspective from Photodetection to Solar Energy Conversion
articles.title_en: First-Principles Insights into Excitonic Physics in 2D Semiconductors
articles.excerpt_original: Chemically and structurally diverse two-dimensional semiconductors exhibit a broad range of excitonic and optical phenomena that have direct implications for optoelectronic functionality. We examine these materials from a first-principles many-body perspective, emphasizing the connection between microscopic excitonic structure and optoelectronic functionality. Reduced symmetry and orbital character produce polarization-selective absorption, while dimensionality, dielectric screening, and exciton fine structure govern binding energies and radiative behavior. In layered systems, interlayer electrostatics and type-II band alignment promote charge separation, whereas exciton-phonon coupling activates indirect optical transitions and shapes temperature-dependent spectra. These mechanisms establish common design principles for excitonic engineering, whereby the dielectric environment, crystal geometry, lattice dynamics, and stacking are used to control exciton properties and tailor optical functionality. This perspective moves beyond description toward the ab initio prediction and design of emerging 2D materials for targeted optoelectronic applications, including polarization-sensitive photodetection and ultrathin solar-energy conversion.
articles.summary_en: This academic perspective examines how symmetry, dielectric screening, band alignment, lattice dynamics, and stacking govern exciton behavior in emerging two-dimensional semiconductors. The findings inform the design of polarization-sensitive photodetectors and ultrathin solar-energy conversion devices.

articles.title_original: Anomalous spin–lattice coupling in a 2D antiferromagnetic semiconductor revealed by surface acoustic Rayleigh waves
articles.title_en: 2D Antiferromagnet Shows Strong Magnetoelastic Coupling
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Magnetic order in van der Waals magnets can strongly influence their lattice dynamics, yet how it affects local and macroscopic manifestations of spin-phonon coupling remains unclear. Optical phonons probe bond-scale exchange modulation and short-range spin correlations, whereas long-wavelength acoustic modes couple to uniform strain fields and are sensitive to renormalization of the macroscopic elastic tensor associated with long-range magnetic order. Experimentally accessing these acoustic excitations in low-dimensional crystals is challenging due to their low energies and the small lateral dimensions of exfoliated samples. Here, we employ Brillouin–Mandelstam scattering spectroscopy to investigate surface acoustic phonons in exfoliated NiPS 3 thin films across the antiferromagnetic transition. Our results show a single Rayleigh surface mode whose phase velocity decreases significantly across the Néel temperature. This anomaly reflects a strong magnetoelastic renormalization of the elastic constants triggered by the onset of antiferromagnetic order. First-principles calculations, combined with continuum finite-element modeling reproduce the Rayleigh-wave dispersion and its magnetic-order–induced shift. The results reveal how microscopic exchange interactions govern the macroscopic elastic response of two-dimensional antiferromagnetic semiconductors, enabling magnetically tunable phononic, magnonic, and strain-mediated spintronic devices.
articles.summary_en: Researchers used Brillouin–Mandelstam spectroscopy and modeling to show that Rayleigh-wave velocity in NiPS₃ thin films drops sharply at the Néel temperature. The finding links magnetic order to macroscopic elastic response, supporting tunable phononic, magnonic and strain-mediated spintronic devices.

articles.title_original: Thermodynamic and kinetic engineering of bi-doped InSe for ultrafast, broadband, and highly stable optoelectronics
articles.title_en: Bismuth-Doped InSe Enables Stable Broadband Optoelectronics
articles.excerpt_original: Two-dimensional (2D) indium selenide (InSe) holds great promise for optoelectronic applications, yet its practical application remains severely limited by high contact resistance, narrow spectral absorption range, and pronounced susceptibility to environmental degradation. Here, a bismuth (Bi) doping strategy is studied to engineer the thermodynamic and kinetic transport properties of InSe field-effect transistors. An optimal nominal Bi content of 25% leads to a pronounced increase in electron density, which effectively narrows the Schottky barrier at the metal–semiconductor interface, yielding a minimized contact resistance of 0.9 kΩ μm and a high field-effect mobility of 412 cm2 V−1 s−1. Concurrently, dopant-induced bandgap renormalization extends the optical response up to 980 nm. This synergistic modulation of interfacial tunneling probability and the joint density of states culminates in a high photoresponsivity and detectivity of 580 A W−1 and 2.52 × 1011 Jones, respectively, while elegantly preserving sub-millisecond response kinetics. Moreover, Bi incorporation suppresses the adsorption of oxygen and moisture on the InSe surface, substantially improving the stability of the unencapsulated devices, which retain 90.2% of their initial photocurrent after 90 days of exposure. This work comprehensively elucidates the interplay between defect dynamics and bandgap engineering, presenting a viable paradigm for robust and broadband 2D optoelectronics.
articles.summary_en: Researchers engineered bismuth-doped indium selenide (InSe) field-effect transistors to reduce contact resistance, extend optical response to 980 nm, and improve environmental stability. Devices achieved high mobility and photoresponsivity while retaining 90.2% of initial photocurrent after 90 days without encapsulation, indicating potential for robust 2D optoelectronic devices.

articles.title_original: Structural Rigidity Enables Amplified Spontaneous Emission in 2D Alkylammonium Tin Perovskites
articles.title_en: Structural Rigidity Enables Amplified Emission in 2D Tin Perovskites
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Two-dimensional tin perovskites are attracting increasing attention for coherent light emission, yet the impact of organic cations on their properties remains poorly understood. Here, we compare the Ruddlesden–Popper (RP) butylammonium tin iodide (BA2SnI4) and Dion–Jacobson (DJ) 1,4-diammoniobutane tin iodide (DABSnI4) perovskites to investigate the impact of the two structural types on their photophysical and optical gain properties. Combining X-ray diffraction and solid-state NMR spectroscopy, we reveal the different templating properties of the mono- and ditopic cations on the long-range structural order and local coordination environment, identifying an unreported phase transition for DABSnI4. The constrained molecular motions in the DJ perovskite provide an increased structural rigidity that also suppresses vibrational modes of the inorganic sublattice. The consequent lower exciton–phonon coupling and exciton binding energy, reduced defectivity, and modulation of the exciton recombination dynamics create favorable conditions to stabilize the population inversion and achieve amplified spontaneous emission (ASE) in DABSnI4, in net contrast with BA2SnI4 where ASE could not be obtained. This work highlights that Dion–Jacobson perovskites can create more rigid structural environments with positive feedback on the photophysical properties, providing a simple but effective design strategy for the synthesis of improved materials for optoelectronic applications.
articles.summary_en: Researchers compared two-dimensional tin perovskites with Ruddlesden–Popper and Dion–Jacobson structures. The more rigid Dion–Jacobson material reduced exciton–phonon coupling, defectivity, and exciton binding energy, enabling amplified spontaneous emission and indicating potential for improved optoelectronic materials.

articles.title_original: Vertical-graphene-decorated carbon nanofiber mats integrated with laser-induced graphene electrodes for piezoresistive pressure sensors
articles.title_en: Vertical Graphene–Carbon Nanofiber Mats Enable Durable Wide-Range Pressure Sensors
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Flexible pressure sensors that combine high sensitivity, a broad operating range, and mechanical durability are needed for wearable electronics, healthcare monitoring, and human–machine interfaces. Here, we report a piezoresistive pressure sensor that integrates a vertical-graphene-decorated carbon nanofiber (VG@CNF) mat with laser-induced graphene (LIG) interdigitated electrodes. The VG@CNF sensing layer was produced by growing spiky vertical graphene (VG) sheets on carbon nanofibers, thereby generating a rough and compressible fibrous network, whereas the LIG electrodes were directly patterned on polyimide by laser scribing to form porous and mechanically robust conductive electrodes. This structural combination promoted pressure-dependent contact formation both within the fibrous mat and at the sensing-layer/electrode interface. Compared with the sensor based on pristine carbon nanofibers without VG, the VG@CNF/LIG device maintained a larger current response over a broader pressure window, exhibiting sensitivities of 0.0142 kPa −1 at 0–60 kPa and 0.0045 kPa −1 at 60–80 kPa, and it remained operable up to 100 kPa. Under 1000 loading–unloading cycles at 100 kPa, the relative current response changed by only 1.7%, indicating good mechanical durability. Proof-of-concept demonstrations, including finger pressing, weight-dependent loading, joint-motion monitoring, and wireless in-shoe detection during running, further confirmed stable and repeatable operation. These results indicate that combining a VG@CNF sensing layer with porous LIG electrodes is an effective structural strategy for improving sensitivity retention at moderate-to-high pressure while preserving a broad working range and mechanical robustness in flexible piezoresistive pressure sensors.
articles.summary_en: Researchers integrated vertical-graphene-decorated carbon nanofiber mats with laser-induced graphene electrodes to create flexible piezoresistive pressure sensors. The device maintained sensitivity across 0–80 kPa, operated up to 100 kPa, and showed only a 1.7% response change after 1,000 loading cycles, with demonstrations in motion monitoring and in-shoe detection.

articles.title_original: High-volumetric-capacitance graphene supercapacitors via DEGDE-mediated GO clay process
articles.title_en: DEGDE-Processed Graphene Electrodes Deliver High Volumetric Capacitance
articles.excerpt_original: A refined and facile strategy is reported for preparing high-volumetric-capacitance graphene supercapacitor electrodes via a diethylene glycol dimethyl ether (DEGDE)-mediated graphene oxide (GO) clay process. Building upon the GO “pottery” concept from our previous work, this method addresses the critical limitation of solvent evaporation and loss of workability by employing DEGDE—a high-boiling-point, high-molecular-weight organic solvent—as a processing aid. This modification preserves the plasticity and uniformity of the GO clay during calendering and thermal reduction, enabling the direct production of dense, self-supporting reduced graphene oxide (rGO) electrode sheets without binders, conductive additives, or extensive purification. The resulting rGO electrodes exhibit a well-defined layered graphene architecture with high packing density. In a symmetric two-electrode configuration with 5 M KOH electrolyte, the electrode delivers a gravimetric specific capacitance of 119.4 ± 4.4 F g ‒1 and a volumetric specific capacitance of 84.0 ± 3.1 F cm ‒3 at 1 mA cm ‒2 , with stable performance across varying currents and excellent reproducibility. This work provides a practical and cost-effective route for high-density graphene electrodes with competitive volumetric performance for compact energy storage applications.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a diethylene glycol dimethyl ether-assisted graphene oxide clay process that produces dense, binder-free reduced graphene oxide electrode sheets. The electrodes achieved 84.0 ± 3.1 F cm⁻³ volumetric capacitance in symmetric supercapacitors, supporting compact energy-storage applications.

articles.title_original: Revealing Strain−Activity Relationship for V2CO2 MXene in Propane Dehydrogenation via p-Band Scaling
articles.title_en: Strain tuning improves MXene catalysts for propane dehydrogenation
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Strain engineering renders two-dimensional MXenes mechanically tunable catalysts. Current work demonstrates that biaxial strain modulates the electronic structure of V2CO2 for propane dehydrogenation (PDH). The reduced p-band center (ε̃p) integrates the p-band center (εp) and p-band width (Wp) into a single dimensionless parameter that serves as a reliable descriptor for C−H activation and H2 desorption. Smaller ε̃p boosts oxygen nucleophilicity and reduces the reaction barriers. This work validates ε̃p as a predictive descriptor for strain-modulated MXene PDH catalysts and provides a quantitative framework for identifying optimal strain conditions.
articles.summary_en: ACS research shows that biaxial strain modulates the electronic structure of V2CO2 MXene catalysts. A reduced p-band descriptor is proposed to predict C–H activation and hydrogen desorption, helping identify optimal strain conditions.

articles.title_original: Hollow bowl‑like MXene/FeNi3 heterostructures for electromagnetic wave absorption and photo‑thermo‑electric conversion
articles.title_en: MXene/FeNi3 Heterostructure Enables High-Performance Radar Absorption and Photothermal Conversion
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Driven by the rapid advancement of modern electronic and wireless technologies , multifunctional electromagnetic wave absorption (EMA) materials are urgently demanded in radar camouflage, 5G/6G communications and energy utilization. However, traditional EMA absorbers face a critical challenge in reconciling the inherent trade-off between high-efficiency absorption and multifunctional integration. Inspired by bioinspired architecture, we construct an open hollow bowl-like MXene/FeNi 3 heterostructure that enables precise modulation of interfacial charge distribution, thereby triggering synergistic effects among interfacial charge transport, oxygen vacancy defects and magnetic interaction. Benefiting from these merits, the optimized MXene/FeNi 3 achieves extraordinarily EMA performances with a minimum reflection loss (RLₘ i ₙ) of − 61.44 dB, an effective absorption bandwidth (EAB) of 6.31 GHz at 1.91 mm, and a Radar Cross section value of − 45.36 dB·m 2 . Furthermore, MXene/FeNi 3 exhibits outstanding photo-thermo-electric conversion performance, attaining a steady surface temperature of 56.7 °C upon 1-sun illumination, maintaining photothermal stability for over 6 h under 2-sun irradiation, and achieving an open-circuit voltage of 225.8 mv and a short-circuit current of 38.9 mA under 1-sun illumination. Importantly, this architecture design strategy is readily extendable to other magnetic systems, including Co, CoFe, CoNi, and FeCoNi, establishing a versatile platform for next-generation multifunctional integrated EMA materials.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a hollow bowl-like MXene/FeNi3 heterostructure with a minimum reflection loss of −61.44 dB and a 6.31 GHz effective absorption bandwidth, indicating potential for radar camouflage and electromagnetic-wave management. The material also demonstrated photothermal and thermoelectric conversion under simulated sunlight, supporting multifunctional energy-utilization applications.

articles.source: Springer Science and Business Media LLC
articles.title_original: Pd-functionalized boron nitride nanotubes for reversible hydrogen storage: a first principles approach
articles.title_en: First-principles study examines palladium-functionalized boron nitride nanotubes for reversible hydrogen storage
articles.summary_en: Researchers model palladium-functionalized boron nitride nanotubes as a potential reversible hydrogen-storage material. The study evaluates storage behavior computationally, without reporting a commercial product or company involvement.

articles.title_original: Tailoring SPR response using MXenes: a theoretical study
articles.title_en: Theoretical study optimizes MXene plasmonic sensors for pesticide detection
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract MXenes are a new family of materials with exciting optical properties that have to the potential to replace conventional plasmonic materials. MXenes with favourable optical properties in literature (Sc2C, Ta2C, Ta4C3, Ti3C2Tx, V2CO2, Nb2CTx, and Ta4C3OH2) and calculated using density functional theory (DFT) (Sc2N and Mo2C) were compared in the current article as surface plasmon resonance (SPR) sensors. The SPR response of four systems were analysed, three systems were in the Kretschmann configuration and one system was in a grating coupled configuration. It was observed that for system 1, with a single continuous MXene layer, the Sc2C MXene showed a sensitivity comparable to a gold film traditionally used in SPR sensors. To further improve the sensitivity, in system 2 and system 3, gold was used in conjunction with the MXenes. Due to the coupling effect of gold and MXene, a very high sensitivity was observed for the SPR sensor with Ti3C2Tx MXene and gold layers. System 4 used MXene in a grating structure on a gold film to improve the sensitivity while using only 2 layers. The structuring effect dominated the SPR response, and the highest sensitivity was seen for Ta2C MXene (182 degree/RIU). The highest figure of merit (FOM) for the grating coupled sensor (204.3 RIU-1) was much higher than the MXene based sensors in the literature. The application of the optimal material, configuration, and thickness was shown by proposing the design of an on-field device for detection of pesticides in water.
articles.summary_en: Density functional theory and optical modeling identify MXene–gold configurations that could improve surface plasmon resonance sensor sensitivity. A grating-coupled Ta₂C design achieved a reported sensitivity of 182°/RIU and figure of merit of 204.3 RIU⁻¹ for potential on-field pesticide detection in water.

articles.title_original: Catalytic MXene implant interfaces reprogram radiation-induced foreign body response to prevent capsular contracture
articles.title_en: MXene-Coated Implants Reduce Radiation-Related Fibrosis in Mice
articles.excerpt_original: Radiotherapy markedly exacerbates foreign body response (FBR) to silicone implants, driving capsular fibrosis and contracture, yet actionable interfacial mechanisms remain insufficiently defined. Here, we engineer an implant-centered Ti 3 C 2 T x MXene-modified PDMS coating (APM) to modulate the redox microenvironment at the tissue–implant interface to reprogram radiotherapy-induced FBR. Oxygen plasma activation and 3-aminopropyltriethoxysilane (APTES) silanization enable covalent anchoring of single-layer MXene nanosheets onto PDMS, yielding a conformal APM film with enhanced hydrophilicity, preserved layered MXene architecture, enzyme-mimicking ROS-scavenging activity, and excellent cytocompatibility. Transcriptomic profiling guides the study, revealing the coordinated downregulation of inflammatory and extracellular matrix remodeling pathways. Mechanistically, interfacial redox regulation dampens NF-κB signaling and reduces endothelial ICAM-1 expression, thereby limiting monocyte adhesion and downstream inflammatory amplification. A tri-culture endothelial–macrophage–fibroblast model further demonstrates that MXene interfaces disrupt pro-inflammatory crosstalk and inhibit myofibroblast activation. In a murine peri-implant irradiation model, APM-coated implants preserve a CD31 + /ICAM-1-low microvasculature, reduce peri-implant pro-inflammatory macrophage accumulation, and significantly decrease capsular thickness and collagen deposition. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that MXene-based catalytic coatings can disrupt the positive feedback loop between radiation injury and fibrotic capsule formation, offering a mechanistically grounded strategy to mitigate implant-associated fibrosis.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a catalytic Ti₃C₂Tₓ MXene coating for silicone implants that scavenges reactive oxygen species and suppresses inflammatory signaling. In cell and mouse models, the coating reduced macrophage accumulation, collagen deposition, and capsular contracture after radiotherapy.

articles.title_original: One-step fabrication of a porous hBN/PDMS composite membrane for breathable and thermally dissipative skin-interface applications
articles.title_en: Porous hBN/PDMS Membrane Combines Breathability with Thermal Dissipation
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Skin-interfaced materials for wearable applications must simultaneously provide effective thermal management, breathability, and mechanical conformability, yet conventional approaches often sacrifice thermal performance for breathability. Here, we report a simple, one-step strategy for the fabrication of a porous hexagonal boron nitride (hBN)/polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) membrane using perfluorohexane (PFH) as a volatile porogen. This approach directly produces a stable porous architecture during casting and curing, eliminating the need for washing, solvent extraction, or post-fabrication treatment. The pore size is tuned based on the curing temperature, which controls the kinetic competition between matrix curing and PFH volatilization. The overall porosity rises from about 15% to 31% with an increase in the PFH content. Importantly, this porous membrane overcomes the conventional trade-off between thermal conductivity and breathability. Although air voids are present, the membrane achieves a thermal conductivity of 0.22 W/m·K, which is comparable to that of the dense form of the composite. This is because the hBN nanoplatelets assemble along the pore walls, forming continuous heat-conduction pathways. Computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations reveal the more effective transfer of heat near the hBN/PDMS composite interface in the porous membrane, which is consistent with the lower heat accumulation observed experimentally. In vivo analysis demonstrates that the porous membrane maintains skin hydration at a stable level of approximately 103–107% and has a mechanical compliance close to that of bare skin, ensuring both physiological and mechanical comfort. These findings establish the proposed one-step fabrication strategy as a material-level foundation for
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a one-step porous hexagonal boron nitride/polydimethylsiloxane membrane using volatile porogen processing, avoiding post-fabrication treatment. The membrane retained thermal conductivity comparable to its dense counterpart while providing skin-like compliance and stable hydration in vivo, supporting breathable wearable skin-interface applications.

articles.title_original: Nitrospinics: Nitride Materials for Spin‐Orbit and Orbital Torques From Memory to Artificial Intelligence
articles.title_en: Nitride Materials Proposed for Spintronics and AI Hardware
articles.excerpt_original: ABSTRACT The exploration of energy‐efficient and functional spintronics has attracted considerable attention. Spin‐orbit and orbital transport have opened new pathways for current‐induced torque generation based on the spin Hall effect. In addition, artificial intelligence computing has been demonstrated using spintronic devices. Further progress of these devices can be anticipated through the development of unique and functional materials, beyond the existing heavy metals and topological systems with strong spin–orbit coupling. The nitride materials exhibit unique chemical, magnetic, and structural versatility, including antiferromagnetism, high thermal stability, and compatibility with diverse device architectures. Here, we propose Nitrospinics as a conceptual and functional framework that exploits nitride materials for applications ranging from spin‐orbit and orbital torque based spintronic devices to artificial intelligence hardware. Using a sputter‐grown multilayer Cr 2 N with MXene‐related layer structure and a nitrogen‐incorporated heavy metal of Pt x N, as prototype systems, we discuss how nitrogen contributes to the structural stability, the orbital torque and spin‐orbit torque generation, and the interfacial orbital to spin conversion. We further outline key challenges and opportunities toward establishing nitride‐based materials for next‐generation computing technologies.
articles.summary_en: The paper introduces “Nitrospinics,” a framework for using nitride materials in spin–orbit and orbital-torque devices, including AI computing hardware. It highlights Cr₂N multilayers and nitrogen-incorporated PtₓN as prototype systems while identifying material and interface challenges for future development.

articles.title_original: Interlayer Registry Controls Polar Topology in Twisted Bilayer h-BN
articles.title_en: Twisted Bilayer h-BN Polar Topology Tuned by Interlayer Registry
articles.excerpt_original: Twisting van der Waals bilayers creates a moir'e stacking field with periodically varying local interlayer registry, enabling spatially patterned polarization. However, a systematic understanding of how this registry-controlled polar topology evolves with twist angle, temperature, and mechanical strain is still lacking. Here, using first-principles-trained deep-potential molecular dynamics simulations, we show that spatially varying interlayer registry governs the polarization texture and can be directly tuned by twist and relative layer deformation. As the twist angle decreases, the moir'e polarization texture evolves from compact, nearly circular vortex-like patterns to extended triangular AB/BA domains. This crossover arises from enhanced lattice relaxation at small twist angles, which expands low-energy, oppositely polarized AB/BA regions and confines in-plane polarization mainly to domain boundaries. Despite this reconstruction, the local in-plane winding remains tied to interlayer registry and persists up to 1000 K, indicating robust topology against thermal fluctuations. We further show that the mechanical response is dictated by whether deformation changes the relative registry: homogeneous deformation of both layers produces only weak distortions, whereas layer-selective deformation strongly reconstructs the moiré polarization texture. A mismatch-matrix registry-mapping model is developed to capture this response, explaining deformation-induced changes in vortex radii at larger twist angles and triangular-domain geometry at smaller twist angles. These results identify interlayer registry as the central control parameter for forming and tuning moir'e polar topology in twisted bilayer h-BN.
articles.summary_en: First-principles-trained molecular dynamics simulations show that interlayer registry controls polarization textures in twisted bilayer hexagonal boron nitride. Twist angle, temperature, and layer-selective strain tune the transition from vortex-like patterns to extended triangular domains, with topology persisting up to 1000 K.

articles.title_original: Competing hysteresis mechanisms in HZO/MoS2 transistors with a metal–ferroelectric–metal–insulator–semiconductor gate stack
articles.title_en: MoS₂ Ferroelectric Transistors Show Competing Hysteresis Effects
articles.excerpt_original: Ferroelectric field-effect transistors based on hafnium oxide offer a versatile platform for advanced memory concepts. Here, we demonstrate a proof-of-concept top-gated Hf0.5Zr0.5O2-based transistor integrating a metal–ferroelectric–metal–insulator–semiconductor (MFMIS) gate stack with a two-dimensional MoS2 channel. The implementation of such an architecture is particularly challenging in MoS2, where the strong sensitivity of the channel to trapped charge can further complicate the balance between ferroelectric switching and charge redistribution within the MFMIS stack. By varying the MFM-to-MIS area ratio and the applied gate-voltage amplitude, we observe a systematic evolution of the transfer hysteresis consistent with competing ferroelectric polarization switching and trap-related contributions. Temperature-dependent measurements, zero-bias write/read experiments, and compact Simulation Program with Integrated Circuit Emphasis modeling provide additional support for this interpretation. Despite the non-optimized gate stack, a substantial ferroelectric contribution to the device response is retained, while retention measurements reveal limitations associated with depolarization and trapping. These results demonstrate the feasibility of MFMIS ferroelectric transistors based on MoS2 and provide a basis for further optimization of their gate-stack design and memory performance.
articles.summary_en: Researchers demonstrated a hafnium–zirconium oxide ferroelectric transistor integrating a two-dimensional MoS₂ channel in an MFMIS gate stack. Measurements identified competing polarization-switching and charge-trapping mechanisms, while retention limitations highlight areas for gate-stack optimization.

articles.title_original: Bipolar Hot Carrier‐Driven Switchable Photocurrent Polarity in Plasmonic‐Functionalized Phototransistor for All‐Optical‐Configured Neuromorphic Computing
articles.title_en: Plasmonic MoS₂ Transistor Enables Switchable Photocurrent Polarity
articles.excerpt_original: ABSTRACT Photocarrier engineering in semiconductors is critical for developing advanced optoelectronic devices. Plasmonic hot carriers enable effective modulation of the photocarrier behavior in semiconductor systems, yet their full potential is restricted by the exploitation of unipolar charges. Herein, by integrating a plasmonic Ag nanoplate layer with an asymmetric MoS 2 transistor, we introduce a plasmon‐enabled photocarrier engineering strategy that achieves vertical bipolar‐hot‐carrier (both hot electrons and hot holes) harvesting and utilization in an n‐type 2D material device for the first time. Hot electron injection into the MoS 2 channel leads to a maximum 50‐fold photoresponsivity enhancement, while hot hole diffusion to the MoS 2 ‐Au electrode interface enables the barrier‐controllable regulation of photoconductivity polarity triggered by optical intensity and wavelength. The multiple‐stimuli‐responsive polarity‐switching characteristic of the hybrid architecture allows for the hardware implementation of an artificial plasmonic neuromorphic system capable of simulating different neural plasticity and performing logical operations with enhanced accuracy. This work presents an innovative framework for the rational design of plasmonic bipolar‐hot‐carrier engineered semiconductor devices with novel functionalities and highlights opportunities for the development of next‐generation optoelectronic intelligence applications.
articles.summary_en: Researchers integrated a silver nanoplate plasmonic layer with an asymmetric MoS₂ transistor to harvest both hot electrons and hot holes. The device achieved up to 50-fold higher photoresponsivity and optically controlled polarity switching, supporting neuromorphic computing functions and logic operations.

articles.title_original: Synergistic Electromagnetic Enhancement and Graphene-Induced Molecular Enrichment for Mid-Infrared Detection of Proteins
articles.title_en: Graphene–Metal Metasurface Enables Ultra-Sensitive Mid-Infrared Protein Detection
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Surface-enhanced infrared absorption spectroscopy (SEIRAs) holds immense potential for trace biomolecular detection. Here, we report a high-performance SEIRAs biosensing platform based on a two-dimensional (2D) monolayer graphene/nanostructured metal metasurface hybrid heterostructure. The platform synergistically couples deep-subwavelength nanoscale electromagnetic hotspots with 100 nm inter-unit gaps with nanomaterial-induced interfacial molecular enrichment. The hybrid sensor amplifies the vibrational fingerprint signals of immunoglobulin G at characteristic amide bands, achieving a low detection concentration down to 3 pM. Furthermore, protein spike-and-recovery assays in unprocessed artificial sweat and urine yield excellent recovery rates. Density functional theory calculations reveal that graphene provides a seamless, non-site-specific π−π physisorption matrix, effectively relieving interfacial steric repulsion and maximizing molecular coverage within plasmonic hotspots. This work provides a robust theoretical framework and an innovative experimental paradigm for the development of next-generation, highly sensitive mid-infrared biosensing technologies.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a graphene/nanostructured-metal metasurface hybrid for surface-enhanced infrared absorption biosensing, detecting immunoglobulin G at concentrations as low as 3 pM. The platform also achieved strong recovery in artificial sweat and urine, supporting potential applications in biomedical sensing.

articles.title_original: Low-power interlayer directional coupling all-optical switch based on graphene-buried polymer waveguide
articles.title_en: Graphene–Polymer Waveguide Enables Low-Power All-Optical Switching
articles.excerpt_original: Three-dimensional photonic integrated circuits provide a pathway toward high-density optical interconnects in the post-Moore era by vertically stacking functional layers. However, interlayer signal switching in such architectures typically relies on complex electrode layouts, which occupy a large footprint and limit further increases in integration density. To address this limitation, a graphene-polymer hybrid all-optical switch using interlayer directional coupling is proposed. All-optical control is achieved via graphene’s photothermal effect. To exploit graphene’s anisotropic absorption, TE polarization is used for the pump to maximize absorption in graphene, whereas TM polarization is used for the signal to minimize graphene-induced loss. For a 190-μm-long active graphene region, the absorption loss for the 980-nm pump is 8.8 dB, while the loss of the 1550-nm signal due to graphene is negligible. The all-optical switch exhibits a 42.3 dB extinction ratio at 3.8 mW pump power. Furthermore, the rise and fall times are 46.1 μs and 107.2 μs, respectively. Our approach provides one feasible pathway to efficient all-optical interlayer signal switching on a polymer platform and offers a compact, low-power, fast-response integrated component for on-chip multilayer interconnects.
articles.summary_en: Researchers proposed a graphene–polymer hybrid switch for interlayer signal routing in three-dimensional photonic integrated circuits. The 190-μm device achieved a 42.3 dB extinction ratio at 3.8 mW pump power, with rise and fall times of 46.1 μs and 107.2 μs, respectively.

articles.title_original: Unveiling giant Rashba splitting in graphene via in situ cryogenic copper adatom deposition and multimodal characterization
articles.title_en: Copper Functionalization Produces Giant Rashba Splitting in Graphene
articles.excerpt_original: Enhancing spin-orbit interaction (SOI) in graphene is a critical step toward realizing graphene-based spintronic devices, yet it has remained experimentally challenging. In this work, we employ in situ cryogenic deposition of copper adatoms on graphene to overcome previous limitations and achieve a controlled, well-defined interface. Through a multimodal approach combining magnetotransport, spin- and angle-resolved photoelectron spectroscopy (spin-ARPES), scanning tunneling microscopy (STM), low-energy electron diffraction (LEED), X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS), and density functional theory (DFT), we provide unambiguous evidence of giant Rashba splitting in graphene. Magnetotransport measurements reveal electron doping, signatures of magnetism, and SOI enhancement, with an extracted Rashba strength of λBR ≈ 1-2 meV at 0.1-0.2 ML Cu coverage. Spin-ARPES directly confirms a giant Rashba splitting of ∼ 50 meV/8 meV for lower/upper Dirac cone at 0.5 ML Cu coverage. Furthermore, ARPES reveals the formation of flat bands near the ¯Γ point, their hybridization with graphene's π states, and quantifies the charge transfer efficiency of η = 0.14. Our comprehensive experimental study, supported by our DFT calculations, resolves the long-standing theory-experiment discrepancy in adatom-induced SOI and establishes copper functionalization as a powerful method for tailoring graphene's spin properties.
articles.summary_en: Researchers used cryogenic copper-adatom deposition and multimodal characterization to demonstrate giant Rashba splitting and enhanced spin–orbit interaction in graphene. The findings establish copper functionalization as a route to tailoring graphene’s spin properties for potential spintronic devices.

articles.title_original: MXene-based microneedle patches for minimally invasive drug delivery: Advances, challenges, and future perspectives
articles.title_en: MXene Microneedle Patches for Minimally Invasive Drug Delivery
articles.summary_en: A review examines MXene-based microneedle patches for minimally invasive drug delivery, covering recent advances, challenges, and future directions. The research highlights the potential of MXene materials to support transdermal therapeutic systems while identifying barriers to broader application.

articles.title_original: Channel decoupling of the memory window in CuInP2S6-gated two-dimensional ferroelectric transistors: conditions, limits, and implications for interface processing
articles.title_en: Study Defines Conditions for Channel-Independent Memory Windows in 2D Ferroelectric Transistors
articles.excerpt_original: We ask which properties of the channel can change the memory window of a metal-ferroelectric-metal-insulator-semiconductor (MFMIS) ferroelectric transistor gated by CuInP 2 S 6 . For a window read at a constant drain current we derive a conditional expression: if the floating gate is an equipotential plane, the ferroelectric carries no charge other than its polarization, and the drain current is the same function of the channel state on both branches of the loop, then the read fixes the channel carrier density at threshold, the surface potential and free channel charge cancel between branches, and the window depends only on the ferroelectric thickness, the switched polarization at the two threshold crossings, and the trapped interface charge. We test it against a simulation of a CuInP 2 S 6 /h-BN/ WSe 2 device in which biaxial strain changes the hole mobility 26-fold; the two agree to within 0.02 percent on a fine sweep grid, and we give closed-form corrections for branch-dependent mobility, unequal capacitor areas, and charge on the ferroelectric side. The channel is not removed from the physics: it enters through the switched polarization, which at threshold is set by the depolarization field and during programming by the charge the stack can supply. The window is therefore channel insensitive only when the channel quantum capacitance at the program extreme exceeds the interlayer capacitance by about tenfold and the read level lies below the onset of switching. Within these conditions the model predicts that compressive strain raises the retained read current 1.90 times without changing the window, and that interface trapping is the channel-side process that limits it. We propose a single-run experiment that can falsify these predictions.
articles.summary_en: Researchers derive conditions under which the memory window in CuInP2S6-gated ferroelectric transistors is independent of channel mobility, supported by simulations of a h-BN/WSe2 device. The model identifies quantum-capacitance and read-level limits, predicts strain-enhanced retained current, and highlights interface trapping as a key constraint.

articles.title_original: Selective Sensing of NH3, NO2, and O2 on Mn-decorated 2D hBN/Silicene Heterostructures
articles.title_en: Mn-Decorated hBN/Silicene Heterostructures Enable Selective Gas Sensing
articles.summary_en: Academic research examines manganese-decorated two-dimensional hBN/silicene heterostructures for selective detection of NH3, NO2, and O2. The work indicates potential sensor applications, but the available excerpt provides no performance metrics or commercialization evidence.

articles.title_original: Kinetically controlled one-step growth of 2D MoS 2 /MoO 2 vertical metal-semiconductor heterostructures
articles.title_en: One-Step CVD Growth of MoS₂/MoO₂ Metal–Semiconductor Heterostructures
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Two-dimensional (2D) heterostructures materials’ family based on layered transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) have always drawn great attention. In particular, 2D metal-semiconductor heterostructures have demonstrated significant potential for high quality electronic devices. However, epitaxial growth of atomically thin metal-semiconductor heterostructures with a pollution-free interface remains a formidable challenge. Herein, a kinetically controlled one-step CVD strategy is developed to directly construct high-quality MoS2/MoO2 vertical metal-semiconductor heterostructures through regulating the sulfurization process of MoO3. As-grown MoS2/MoO2 heterostructures exhibit the non-centrosymmetric characteristic and excellent piezoelectric performance. Benefiting this heterostructure interface, the conductive nano-tip/MoS2/MoO2 devices exhibit stable bipolar resistive switching behavior and excellent endurance. This heterostructure growth strategy not only avoids the interfacial contamination and poor interlayer contact commonly associated with mechanical stacking and two-step CVD processes, but can also, in principle, be extended to other 2D vertical heterostructures, providing a promising platform for the integration of volatile resistive switching devices and piezoelectric sensors.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a kinetically controlled, one-step CVD process to grow clean-interface vertical MoS₂/MoO₂ heterostructures. The materials showed piezoelectric performance and stable resistive switching, supporting potential applications in semiconductor devices, memory, and sensors.

articles.title_original: Stress-controlled transfer of high-mobility organic semiconductor nanosheets for thin-film transistors
articles.title_en: Stress-Controlled Transfer Improves Organic TFT Fabrication
articles.excerpt_original: Organic thin-film transistors (TFTs) are key components for large-area and mechanically flexible electronic devices, and reliable fabrication methods beyond direct physical vapor deposition (PVD) are required, particularly for technical and non-planar surfaces. We fabricated organic TFTs by transferring organic small-molecule nanosheets. During the release and transfer process, the nanosheets experience significant mechanical stress, leading to plastic deformation or phase changes that can be quantified by X-ray diffraction (XRD). In accordance with classical bending theory, the mechanical stress can be significantly reduced by limiting the nanosheet thickness to 30 nm or less. Using this optimized thickness, we directly compare transferred nanosheets with thin films prepared by PVD on self-assembled monolayer (SAM)-functionalized bottom contacts. TFTs fabricated with transferred dinaphtho[2,3-b:2',3'-f]thieno[3,2-b]thiophene (DNTT) nanosheets exhibit a mobility of 0.32 cm2/V s and a subthreshold swing of 114 mV/dec, approaching state-of-the-art TFTs fabricated by direct PVD, which exhibit here a mobility of 0.42 cm2/V s. XRD indicates that transferred DNTT nanosheets exhibit superior crystalline order on the contacts compared to films grown by direct PVD. However, the PVD growth on the gate dielectric, i.e., on SAM-passivated Al2O3, is slightly better than on the sacrificial polymer layer. These results indicate that the transport properties of the transferred nanosheets are not primarily limited by the transfer process itself, but rather by the thin-film growth on the sacrificial water-soluble polymer layer. Transferable nanosheets have applications in hybrid devices and devices with unconventional geometries, e.g., non-planar transistors or devices containing free-st
articles.summary_en: Researchers demonstrated transferable organic semiconductor nanosheets for thin-film transistors, reducing transfer-induced stress by limiting thickness to 30 nm or less. Transferred DNTT devices achieved 0.32 cm²/V·s mobility, approaching directly deposited films at 0.42 cm²/V·s, supporting flexible and non-planar electronics.

articles.title_original: High-Fidelity Electrochemistry with Ultraclean Graphene Electrodes
articles.title_en: Oxygen-Free CVD Produces High-Fidelity Graphene Electrodes
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract The electrochemical performance of CVD graphene electrodes has remained inconsistent and often inferior to that of exfoliated graphene, limiting their utility in analytical applications. This variability is widely attributed to structural disorder, but the dominant source remains unclear. Here, we show that amorphous carbon contamination introduced during synthesis is the primary factor governing the electrochemical behavior of CVD graphene. By eliminating this disorder during growth through oxygen-free CVD (OF-CVD), we obtain graphene electrodes that exhibit intrinsic and highly reproducible electrochemical behavior. Compared with conventional and commercial graphene, these electrodes display substantially enhanced heterogeneous electron-transfer kinetics, reduced charge-transfer resistance, and improved detection limits across both outer- and inner-sphere redox systems. Notably, they exhibit consistent anodic peak potentials across wide concentration ranges, nearly eliminating the concentration-dependent potential shifts characteristic of both glassy carbon and commercial/contaminated graphene electrodes. Further, microelectrode array architectures fabricated from this material suppress non-Faradaic background currents and exhibit steady-state diffusion behavior consistent with electrochemical theory, with improved signal-to-noise ratios. Together, these results establish that extrinsic carbon disorder has limited the electrochemical performance of CVD graphene to date. The removal of amorphous carbon reveals defect-free graphene’s intrinsic electrochemical behavior and enables a reproducible, high-performance electrode platform, providing a clear pathway for reliable graphene-based electrochemical systems.
articles.summary_en: Researchers show that amorphous carbon contamination, rather than structural disorder alone, drives the inconsistent electrochemical performance of CVD graphene. Oxygen-free CVD graphene electrodes deliver reproducible electron-transfer kinetics, lower charge-transfer resistance, improved detection limits, and better signal-to-noise in microelectrode arrays.

articles.title_en: Ionic Liquid-Functionalized Doped MXene Nanosheets Enhance Lubrication

articles.title_original: A first-principles investigation into the structural, electronic, and optical properties of two-dimensional BN and diamond-like carbon intercalation systems, as modified by fluorination and hydrogenation
articles.title_en: First-Principles Study Examines Fluorinated and Hydrogenated 2D BN and Carbon Intercalation Systems

articles.title_original: Strain‐Controlled Pt Single‐Atom Catalysts on Crumpled MXene Supports for Highly Active Hydrogen Evolution
articles.title_en: Strain-Engineered MXene Catalyst Boosts Hydrogen Evolution
articles.excerpt_original: ABSTRACT Strain engineering offers a powerful means to regulate the electronic structure and catalytic behavior of active metal sites, yet a general framework linking strain to electrocatalytic performance remains elusive beyond the conventional d‐band model. Here we report crumpled double‐transition‐metal MXene nanosheets (Mo 2 TiC 2 T x ) decorated with Pt single atoms, in which a tunable strain field is introduced through a physical diaphragm balloon method. The resulting cMo 2 TiC 2 T x ‐Pt SA catalyst exhibits outstanding alkaline hydrogen evolution performance, requiring overpotentials of only 24.9 and 75.5 mV to reach 10 and 50 mA cm −2 , respectively, together with a mass activity of 11 859 mA mgPt −1 , around 178‐fold higher than commercial Pt/C, a Tafel slope of 31.61 mV dec −1 and excellent durability. In situ spectroscopy and density functional theory calculations show that the ordered long‐range strain field around isolated Pt sites accelerates interfacial water activation while preserving near‐optimal H adsorption, thereby facilitating H 2 release. The resulting catalyst delivered a high current density of 3 A cm −2 at a low voltage of 1.98 V and maintained stable operation at 1000 mA cm −2 for over 500 h. These performance metrics underscore the potential of cMo 2 TiC 2 T x ‐Pt SA for industrial applications.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed Pt single-atom catalysts on crumpled MXene supports, achieving low overpotentials, high mass activity, and stable operation for more than 500 hours. The findings indicate a potentially scalable route to high-performance alkaline hydrogen production, although no commercial partner or company is identified.

articles.title_original: Recovery-Induced Spatial Engineering of Au/MXene Nanoarchitectures for Direct Ion-to-Electrode Conversion
articles.title_en: MXene Membranes Convert Gold Waste into Binder-Free Electrocatalytic Electrodes
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Creating direct pathways that transform dissolved metal waste into functional architecture is central to sustainable nanomanufacturing and circular materials design. Here, we report a redox-driven strategy for the direct conversion of gold (Au) ions from electronic waste into spatially organized Au/MXene nanoarchitectures and electrocatalytic membranes. Ti3C2Tx MXene nanosheets exhibit an Au uptake capacity of 3720 mg g–1 at 1 ppm, together with high selectivity in the presence of excess competing metal ions. Mechanistic studies reveal that the Au capture is coupled with spontaneous interfacial redox conversion, where ∼91% of Au(III) ions are reduced in situ into metallic Au nanoparticles on the MXene surface. Importantly, performing the recovery process in a dispersed colloidal state enables recovery-induced interlayer assembly, producing homogeneous Au distributions throughout the MXene framework after vacuum-assisted membrane formation. In contrast to surface-confined deposition in conventional filtration architectures, the interlayer nanoarchitecture preserves ion-transport pathways and maximizes catalytic accessibility. We further show that ultratrace Au concentrations promote the formation of highly dispersed confined Au domains, enabling efficient electrocatalytic membranes despite substantially lower gold loading. The resulting membranes function directly as flexible binder-free electrodes without additional refining, metal stripping, or catalyst deposition steps. This work establishes a recovery-as-fabrication strategy in which dissolved metal ions are directly transformed into functional nanoarchitectures through coupled redox reduction, confined nucleation, and interlayer assembly.
articles.summary_en: Researchers demonstrated a redox-driven method that captures dissolved gold ions from electronic waste and assembles them into Au/MXene membrane architectures. The flexible membranes operate directly as binder-free electrodes, combining metal recovery with catalyst fabrication without refining or additional deposition.

articles.title_original: Stabilization and Transformation of MXenes into Flexible and Thermal Oxidation-Resistant Non-van der Waals solids via Vapor-Phase Chemical Intercalation
articles.title_en: Vapor-phase intercalation produces flexible, oxidation-resistant MXene solids
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Non-van der Waals (non-vdW) solids derived from MXenes exhibit attractive physical and chemical properties but are usually limited by the irreversible phase transformation of MXenes into rocksalt structures at high temperatures. Herein, we develop a vapor-phase chemical intercalation strategy mediated by high-vapor-pressure zinc (Zn) to efficiently stabilize the transition metals (Ti, Nb, and V) with unsaturated d-orbitals in MXenes. This stabilization facilitates subsequent interlayer bonding via reaction with various metal vapors (Al, Ga, and In) at elevated temperatures, yielding a family of well-defined non-vdW solids with ultrathin layered structures. Moreover, this strategy is readily scalable, enabling the fabrication of a continuous non-vdW Al–Ti3C2 film featuring a heterogeneous architecture with a reconstructed MAX-like bonded region and a locally unbonded MXene region. These structural features endow the non-vdW Al–Ti3C2 film with exceptional mechanical flexibility, high-temperature oxidation resistance at 800 °C in air, and an electrical conductivity of ∼10 000 S cm–1. Consequently, the film demonstrates an electromagnetic interference shielding effectiveness of up to 47.9 dB at a thickness of 5 μm, along with durable infrared stealth performance under prolonged exposure at 500 °C for 48 h.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a scalable vapor-phase chemical intercalation method to stabilize MXenes and form ultrathin non-van der Waals solids. An Al–Ti3C2 film combined flexibility, oxidation resistance at 800 °C, high conductivity, 47.9 dB EMI shielding, and infrared stealth performance at 500 °C for 48 hours.

articles.title_original: MXene Ti3C2Tx-ZnO heterostructure for Q-switched and mode-locked fiber laser at 1.5 µm
articles.title_en: MXene–ZnO heterostructure enables Q-switched and mode-locked fiber lasers
articles.excerpt_original: This work demonstrates a saturable absorber (SA) based on Ti 3 C 2 T x -zinc oxide (ZnO), for Q-switched and mode-locked generation in an erbium-doped fiber laser (EDFL) cavity. The SA was fabricated using a solution-casting method, in which both materials were mixed to form a thin-film structure. The UV–vis-NIR spectroscopy and twin-balanced detector technique reveal a 0.4 a.u. absorbance and 10.1% modulation depth, indicating its potential as SA. The film was incorporated in the EDFL cavity, initiating a Q-switched and mode-locked laser in the 1.5 µm regime. The Ti 3 C 2 T x -ZnO generates Q-switched pulses at a center wavelength of 1559.8 nm, and the center wavelength blue-shifts to 1558.65 nm when the laser operates in the mode-locking regime. The minimum pulse width of the Q-switched and mode-locked pulses is 6.56 µs and 3.91 ps, respectively. The developed SA can also be used for pulsed laser generation in another near-to-mid-infrared regime, including 1-, 1.33–, and 2-µm.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a Ti₃C₂Tₓ MXene–ZnO thin-film saturable absorber for erbium-doped fiber lasers operating near 1.5 µm. The device produced Q-switched pulses with a minimum width of 6.56 µs and mode-locked pulses as short as 3.91 ps, indicating potential for broader near- to mid-infrared pulsed-laser applications.

articles.summary_en: A technical monograph outlines a proposed neuromorphic-chip architecture combining topological 2D materials, memristive arrays, graphene plasmonic interconnects, encapsulated self-healing devices, and phononic thermal management. bulletin.title: Graphene Weekly Bulletin — Week ending 2026-10-18
bulletin.introduction: Commercial activity is concentrating around scale-up, regional access and downstream integration: Skeleton’s Siemens-led financing supports energy-storage expansion, while graphene businesses pursue Middle East partnerships, manufacturing options, acquisition and application-led orders. Evidence for several initiatives remains preliminary, limiting conclusions on volumes or revenue. Research continues to broaden graphene’s addressable roles in protective coatings, conductive and thermal materials, electronics and infrastructure. A recurring technical pattern is narrow formulation and processing windows, with dispersion, loading and interface control determining whether laboratory gains translate into durable performance.
